Behind "testable" sits operationalization: turning a fuzzy concept ("better", "engagement", "reasoning ability") into a measurable variable. Every operationalization is a choice that can be wrong, so state it explicitly. A well-posed empirical question names an estimand: the population, the intervention or comparison, the outcome measure, and the summary (mean difference, hazard ratio, AUROC gap). The "under condition Z, measured by M" rewrite in the panel is exactly this.

Also decide the smallest effect size of interest before collecting data. It sets the sample size, and it stops you from celebrating a statistically detectable but practically irrelevant difference. Finally, label work as exploratory (generating hypotheses) or confirmatory (testing one fixed in advance); the same p-value means very different things in each.

Each step hides a trap. "Map assumptions" is where you write down what must hold for your test to be informative; a causal diagram (nodes = variables, arrows = suspected influences) forces this. A key logical point, the Duhem-Quine problem: you never test a hypothesis alone, only the hypothesis plus auxiliary assumptions (the data pipeline is correct, the metric is valid, the sample is representative). A failed prediction therefore does not tell you which one broke.

Analysis choices made after seeing data multiply the number of implicit tests you ran. Gelman and Loken (2013) called this the garden of forking paths: even without deliberate p-hacking, a flexible analysis can produce a convincing story from noise. The remedy is to fix the decision rule (what result would change your mind?) before you look.

Randomization works because it makes treatment assignment independent of everything else, including unmeasured variables, so the difference in group means is an unbiased estimate of the average treatment effect. Note "in expectation": any single small trial can still be imbalanced, which is why stratified or blocked randomization and balance checks exist.

In ML, "strong baseline" means tuned with the same budget as your method; many apparent gains vanish when the baseline gets equal hyperparameter search (Melis et al. 2017 showed this for language models). Power analysis: to detect a standardized difference d between two groups with 80% power at a two-sided alpha of 0.05, you need roughly 16/d² samples per group (d = 0.5 gives about 64). Smaller true effects need quadratically more data, which is why underpowered studies are so common.

Research groups fail in predictable ways, and most are about information flow rather than talent. Psychological safety, a term popularized by Amy Edmondson (1999), means people believe they can voice doubts without penalty; it matters because errors in experiments are usually noticed by someone who then stays quiet.

Two concrete practices make the roles in the panel real. First, a pre-mortem: before running an expensive experiment, everyone writes down how it will have failed and what they would have wished they had checked. Second, independent review of the analysis code and data splits by someone who did not write them; most leakage bugs are invisible to the author. "Hero culture" shows up as a bus factor of one: if only one person can reproduce a result, the result is not yet established.

Choose tests by the question and by what the test actually compares. The t-test compares means; prefer Welch's version, which does not assume equal variances, as the default. With moderate samples the t-test is fairly robust to non-normality because of the central limit theorem, so "data are not normal" alone is a weak reason to abandon it. Mann-Whitney U tests whether a random draw from one group tends to exceed one from the other (stochastic dominance); it equals a median comparison only if the two distributions have the same shape. Chi-square needs expected cell counts of about 5 or more; Fisher's exact test does not. The bootstrap (resampling with replacement) approximates sampling distributions when no formula exists. Effect size (e.g. Cohen's d, a mean difference in units of pooled standard deviation) answers "how big", which a p-value cannot.

A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true; it is not the probability the hypothesis is true. If you run m independent tests at alpha = 0.05 with no real effects, the chance of at least one false positive is 1 - 0.95^m, already about 64% for m = 20. Bonferroni (use alpha/m) controls that family-wise error but is conservative; Benjamini and Hochberg (1995) controls the false discovery rate, the expected fraction of declared discoveries that are false, which suits exploratory screens.

Small samples also exaggerate: among the estimates that happen to reach significance in a low-power study, the effect is overstated on average (Gelman and Carlin's "Type M" error, 2014). In ML the equivalent is picking the best of many runs or configurations and reporting it as the expected performance.

Anscombe's quartet (1973) is the classic argument for plotting first: four datasets with nearly identical means, variances, correlation (about 0.82) and fitted line, yet one is curved, one has an outlier, one is a vertical stack with a single leverage point. Summary statistics discard exactly the structure that matters.

Distinguish standard deviation (spread of the data) from standard error (uncertainty of the estimate, roughly SD/√n); papers that blur them make results look more certain than they are. Assumption checks are about what the method needs: independence is the one most often violated (repeated measures per user, per patient, per prompt), and it makes naive standard errors too small; use clustered or hierarchical methods. For sensitivity analysis, specification-curve analysis (Simonsohn et al. 2020) plots the result across all defensible analysis choices, showing whether the conclusion depends on one arbitrary path.

The mantra maps to concrete behaviors. Precise: state the estimand and the metric before the result. Rigorous: pre-specified analysis, held-out test data touched once, multiple seeds. Honest: report all experiments you ran, including failures, and label post-hoc findings as exploratory; Feynman's formulation (1974) is that the first principle is not to fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool. Humble: state the scope of the claim, covering which population, which model scale, which dataset, because external validity is usually narrower than the abstract implies. The Open Science Collaboration (2015) attempted to replicate 100 psychology studies and found that roughly a third to a half reproduced the original significant effects, depending on the criterion, which is the cost of skipping these habits. Useful: prefer effects that change a decision.
ml-research-01.further: Common misconception: statistical significance is not evidence of importance, and non-significance is not evidence of no effect; a wide confidence interval just means you could not tell. Another gotcha is treating the sequence "explore, then test" as one pass over the same data: once the data suggested the hypothesis, it cannot also confirm it, which is why a held-out split or a fresh sample matters. This page is the philosophy behind the rest of the book: cross-validation and the debugging checklist are the same discipline (keep the test honest) applied to models, and the correlation-versus-causation page is the same humility applied to claims.

panels: Shape discipline is the single most useful habit in deep learning code. Frameworks like PyTorch store tensors as flat memory plus strides (how far to jump per axis), so transposing or slicing usually creates a view, not a copy; a view can be non-contiguous, which is why some operations demand .contiguous(). Broadcasting aligns shapes from the trailing axis and treats size-1 axes as stretchable: (B,T,D) + (D,) works, but (n,) minus (n,1) silently produces an (n,n) matrix, a classic bug that raises no error. Common dtypes are float32, and bfloat16 or float16 for speed and memory on accelerators (bfloat16 keeps float32's exponent range but has fewer mantissa bits). Debug trick: use distinct, unequal sizes (B=3, T=5, D=7) in a test so any axis mix-up shows up as an error.

Matrix multiplication (n×d)(d×h) costs about 2·n·d·h floating-point operations, and it is the dominant cost of nearly every neural network. Geometrically, a dot product is |x||w|cos(θ): it grows with both length and alignment, which is why attention uses dot products as similarity and why cosine similarity normalizes lengths away. Matrix multiplication is associative but not commutative, and associativity changes cost: for a (1000×10)(10×1000)(1000×1) chain, computing right-to-left costs far less than left-to-right. Norm choice has consequences: L2 distance is rotation-invariant and smooth, L1 is robust to outliers and favors sparsity. In very high dimensions, pairwise distances between random points concentrate (they become nearly equal), which weakens nearest-neighbor intuition and is one reason embeddings are often compared by angle.

Backpropagation is reverse-mode automatic differentiation. For a layer y = f(x), the backward pass computes the vector-Jacobian product: dL/dx = Jᵀ · dL/dy, where J is the matrix of partial derivatives of y with respect to x. The full Jacobian is never formed. The backward pass costs roughly 2x the forward pass and needs the stored forward activations, which is why training memory scales with depth and batch size, and why activation checkpointing (recompute instead of store) exists.

For gradient descent on a smooth quadratic whose curvature (largest Hessian eigenvalue) is λ_max, the step size must satisfy η < 2/λ_max or the iteration diverges. Ill-conditioned problems (very different curvatures along different directions) force a small η, making progress slow along flat directions; this is what momentum and adaptive optimizers address.

The panel's variance uses 1/n, which is the population formula. Estimating variance from a sample uses 1/(n-1) (Bessel's correction) because the sample mean is itself fitted to the data. Expectations are usually approximated by Monte Carlo: average f over n samples, with error shrinking like 1/√n, so 4x more samples halves the noise. Softmax is shift-invariant (adding a constant to all logits changes nothing), so implementations subtract the max logit, or use log-sum-exp, to avoid overflow in exp. Dividing logits by a temperature T before softmax sharpens (T<1) or flattens (T>1) the distribution.

The unifying idea: each distribution pairs with a loss through maximum likelihood. Gaussian noise gives squared error, Bernoulli gives binary cross-entropy, categorical gives cross-entropy. Choosing a loss is choosing a noise model.

Cross-entropy H(y, p) = -Σ y_i log p_i splits as the entropy of y plus the KL divergence KL(y‖p); with one-hot labels the entropy is zero, so minimizing it is exactly maximum likelihood on the labels. Combined with softmax, the gradient with respect to the logits is simply p - y (frameworks fuse log-softmax into the loss for stability, which is why PyTorch's CrossEntropyLoss wants raw logits). MSE corresponds to Gaussian noise with fixed variance and is outlier-sensitive; Huber loss turns linear beyond a threshold.

Regularization has a Bayesian reading: L2 penalizes like a Gaussian prior on weights, L1 like a Laplace prior (whose sharp peak at zero yields exact zeros). For Adam, L2 added to the loss is not equivalent to weight decay; AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) decouples them, which is the standard form today.

Treat the checklist as an executable debugging routine. Three checks catch a large fraction of bugs. First, expected initial loss: with K balanced classes and a sensibly initialized model, cross-entropy should start near ln(K) (about 6.9 for 1000 classes); if it starts far from that, initialization, label alignment or loss wiring is off. Second, overfit one tiny batch: a correct model with a correct training loop can drive loss to nearly zero on 10 examples; if it cannot, there is a bug, not a tuning issue. Third, check reduction semantics: sum versus mean over batch or time changes the effective learning rate, and padding must be masked out. Question 6 also covers applying softmax twice, a common bug.

Each failure has a fingerprint. Vanishing gradients: backprop multiplies one Jacobian per layer, so the gradient norm behaves like ρ^L for typical per-layer gain ρ; sigmoid's derivative peaks at 0.25, so deep sigmoid stacks shrink gradients geometrically. Exploding gradients are the ρ>1 case; the standard fix is clipping the global gradient norm to a fixed threshold. Residual connections and normalization layers keep ρ near 1.

Numerical failures are separate: log(0) gives -inf and then NaN, exp of a large logit overflows, and float16 has a narrow range, so mixed-precision training uses loss scaling (multiply the loss by a large constant before backprop, then unscale). A related trap: averaging over the wrong axis (mean over the batch when you meant per-token) silently changes both the loss scale and which examples dominate. Always print shapes and a few values, not just metrics.
ml-deep-01.further: A frequent misconception is that math background is needed for derivations; in practice, most failures come from bookkeeping: shapes, axes, reduction modes, and logits versus probabilities. The cure is mechanical: assert shapes, test on tiny batches, and compare against a numerical gradient (finite differences) when writing a custom operation. Connect this page forward: softmax and cross-entropy return in classification metrics and in language-model training, attention is a softmax over dot products, and the gradient-descent rule here is what optimizers like Adam elaborate on in the next page. Keep the distinction between the loss you optimize (smooth, differentiable) and the metric you care about (often not) in mind throughout.

Why does the nonlinearity matter? Without it, two linear layers collapse: W₂(W₁x) = (W₂W₁)x, a single linear map, so depth adds nothing. With it, the universal approximation theorems (Cybenko 1989, Hornik 1991) say even one hidden layer can approximate any continuous function on a compact set, but that is an existence result: it says nothing about how many units are needed or whether gradient descent finds them. Depth is valuable because composition builds features efficiently.

The training loop is five steps: forward pass, loss, backward pass (compute gradients), optimizer step (update weights), and zeroing the gradients for the next batch. The loss surface is non-convex; in high dimensions, saddle points (flat in some directions, curved in others) are more common obstacles than bad local minima (Dauphin et al. 2014), and over-parameterized networks tend to have many good solutions.

An embedding layer is equivalent to multiplying a one-hot vector by a matrix of shape (V×D), but implemented as a row lookup; the gradient is sparse (only rows used in the batch receive updates). Convolution applies the same small kernel at every position, so parameters are K·K·C_in·C_out regardless of image size, and the output is translation-equivariant: shift the input and the feature map shifts equally. Output length along one axis is floor((H + 2P - K)/S) + 1 for padding P, kernel K, stride S.

Batch norm normalizes each channel using batch mean and variance, then applies a learned scale and shift; at inference it uses running averages, so train and eval behave differently (a classic bug is forgetting eval mode). Inverted dropout rescales kept activations by 1/(1-p) during training so inference is unchanged.

A mini-batch gradient is an unbiased but noisy estimate of the full gradient; its variance falls roughly as 1/batch size, so larger batches give diminishing returns per step. The linear scaling rule (Goyal et al. 2017) for SGD multiplies the learning rate by k when batch size grows k times, with warmup, up to a limit. Adam keeps exponential moving averages of the gradient (m, beta1 = 0.9) and squared gradient (v, beta2 = 0.999), and steps by η · m̂/(√v̂ + ε), where hats mean bias-corrected; AdamW is the usual choice for transformers.

The 70/15/15 split is convention, not law. With millions of examples a few thousand validation examples suffice; what matters is that the test set's confidence interval (for accuracy, a half-width of about 2√(p(1-p)/n)) is narrower than the differences you care about.

Each block encodes an inductive bias, an assumption about the data that narrows the functions the model prefers. Convolution assumes locality and translation equivariance; embeddings assume discrete symbols deserve learned dense coordinates; recurrence assumes order matters sequentially; attention lets each position decide dynamically which others to read. Strong biases help when data is scarce; weaker ones pay off with large-scale pretraining (vision transformers, Dosovitskiy et al. 2020, relied on very large datasets).

Normalization choice follows the same logic. Batch norm depends on batch statistics, which is awkward for small batches and sequence models; layer norm normalizes across the features of each single example, so it is independent of batch size and is standard in transformers. Why batch norm helps is still debated: the original "internal covariate shift" explanation was challenged (Santurkar et al. 2018) in favor of smoother loss landscapes.

Dead ReLU: if a unit's pre-activation is negative for all inputs, its output and gradient are exactly zero, so it never recovers. Initialization matters here: He initialization (He et al. 2015) draws weights with variance 2/fan_in for ReLU networks, and Glorot/Xavier (2010) uses 2/(fan_in + fan_out) for tanh-like units; both aim to keep activation and gradient scale roughly constant across layers.

Gradient clipping (usually by global norm, popularized for recurrent nets by Pascanu et al. 2013) rescales the whole gradient if its norm exceeds a threshold. Batch norm with tiny batches yields noisy statistics, and train-time and test-time behavior diverge; GroupNorm (Wu and He 2018) avoids batch dependence. Compute standardization statistics on the training split only.

Treat the checklist as a ladder: when training misbehaves, climb it in order. Karpathy's widely cited 2019 "Recipe for Training Neural Networks" is a good model: become familiar with the data first; build the simplest end-to-end pipeline and fix seeds; verify initial loss; overfit a single batch; then add regularization and tune. Useful monitors beyond loss: gradient norm per layer, and the ratio of update size to weight size (a heuristic from the cs231n course is roughly 1e-3; if far from that, the learning rate is suspect). Sweep the learning rate on a log scale rather than a linear one, because training quality typically changes over orders of magnitude. Item 8, "can a simpler baseline do this?", is the most skipped and often the most informative: a logistic regression or gradient-boosted trees may match the network.
ml-deep-02.further: Misconceptions to drop: more layers does not mean better, and a big train-versus-validation gap does not automatically mean you should shrink the model; in modern over-parameterized networks the validation metric can keep improving while the gap exists, so judge by validation performance, not by the gap alone (see the debugging page). Dropout and batch norm interact awkwardly, and many large transformers use little or no dropout during pretraining because data is plentiful. This page supplies the vocabulary for the transformer pages later in the book: the embedding layer, layer norm, residual structure and AdamW introduced here all reappear there, and the training curves discussed here are what the scaling-law and distributed-training pages try to predict and keep stable.

Be precise about what cross-validation estimates: not the quality of one final model, but the expected performance of a training procedure (model, preprocessing, hyperparameter rule) applied to datasets of the size of the training folds. Each fold model trains on (k-1)/k of the data, so the estimate is slightly pessimistic for small k; leave-one-out has the least bias but its fold models are nearly identical, so errors are highly correlated and variance of the average can be high. There is no unbiased estimator of the variance of k-fold CV error (Bengio and Grandvalet 2004), which means any ± you report is approximate.

In practice, refit the chosen procedure on all non-test data and evaluate once on the untouched test set; CV cannot replace that check because your selections have already adapted to the folds.

The ten variants differ in what they hold out. K-fold treats rows as exchangeable. Stratified K-fold keeps label proportions per fold, which matters when a fold could otherwise contain zero positives. Nested CV exists because picking the best of many hyperparameter settings by CV score makes that score optimistically biased (Cawley and Talbot 2010): an inner loop selects hyperparameters, an outer loop scores the whole selection procedure. Cost is multiplicative: 5 outer folds, 5 inner folds and a 20-point grid is 500 fits plus 5 refits.

Group variants ensure all rows of a patient, user or document land in the same fold. Time-series splits train on an expanding (or sliding) past window and validate on the future; when labels look ahead in time, add a gap or purge (embargo) period between train and validation so overlapping horizons do not leak.

The decision flow boils down to one principle: the validation split must mimic the dependence between train and deployment. Ask what a new instance means at deployment: a new patient, a new day, a new document? Then split by that unit. If several conditions apply, apply all: imbalanced and grouped data call for stratified group K-fold; temporal data with repeated users needs time-aware splits that also respect groups, and the strictest requirement usually dominates.

Data size affects the choice of k and holdout. With large data the sampling error of a single holdout is small: for 10,000 validation examples and accuracy near 0.9, the standard error is about √(0.9·0.1/10000) = 0.3 percentage points, so extra folds buy little and cost much. With small data, that error is large and repetition helps.

The most instructive leak is feature selection done outside the loop. Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman (The Elements of Statistical Learning, section 7.10.2) show that selecting the "best" features using all labels and then cross-validating a classifier can report strongly better-than-chance accuracy on data whose labels are pure noise, because the selection step already saw the validation labels. Any step that learns from data (scaling, imputation, PCA, target encoding, resampling, feature selection) must be fitted inside each training fold; in scikit-learn this means wrapping everything in a Pipeline.

Another subtle point: the standard deviation across folds understates uncertainty, because training sets overlap heavily and fold scores are correlated; Nadeau and Bengio (2003) proposed a corrected resampled t-test for comparing models. Near-duplicates (augmented images, paraphrased text, repeated records) behave like group leakage, so deduplicate or cluster before splitting.

"Define the unit of prediction" is the key sentence. If a model scores patients but rows are visits, the unit is the patient. Hashing the group ID into a fold number keeps splits stable as data grows. Persist the fold indices and seed.

Use paired comparison: evaluate competing models on identical folds and compare the per-fold differences, which have much lower variance than comparing two separately computed averages. For uncertainty, bootstrap by group (resample whole patients, not rows) to respect dependence. The "final untouched test set" is consumed by use: each time you look at it and change something, it becomes a validation set. Touch it once, or rotate in a fresh sample.

Read the table as a tradeoff of cost, variance, and realism. Holdout is cheapest but has the highest variance; K-fold uses k fits and lowers variance; repeated K-fold multiplies that by the repeat count. Group K-fold and LOGO estimate performance on unseen groups, which is typically lower than plain K-fold on the same data. That is realism: plain K-fold answers a different question (new rows of known patients). The two numbers can differ dramatically, so the one matching deployment is the right one to report.

Time-series splits answer "how would this have done if deployed then", and a drop in later folds is itself a diagnostic of drift. For nested CV the honest reading is that its outer score estimates the whole procedure including tuning, not any specific hyperparameter setting.
ml-classical-07.further: Misconception: cross-validation improves the model. It only measures; it does not train a better model than a single fit does (though it informs choices). Another: more folds is always better; beyond 5-10, gains are small and variance behavior is subtle. Gotchas: calibration and thresholds must also be chosen without peeking at the evaluation fold; early stopping on the validation fold biases the score upward, so use a separate inner split. For LLM and deep-learning work, full CV is rarely affordable, so the same ideas appear as fixed splits with deduplication against pretraining data (contamination checks). This page connects directly to the imbalanced-class and debugging pages, whose leakage warnings are the same issue in different clothes.

panels: AUROC equals the probability that a random positive outscores a random negative (ties count half); This is the normalized Mann-Whitney U statistic. It depends only on score ranks, so it says nothing about calibration. Its weakness under rarity comes from the false positive rate, FP/(FP+TN): with a million negatives, an FPR of 1% still means 10,000 false alarms, yet ROC looks excellent. AUPRC (area under precision versus recall) puts those false alarms into the denominator of precision, so it penalizes them; its no-skill baseline is the prevalence, which is why values are not comparable across datasets. Linear interpolation between PR points is misleading (Davis and Goadrich 2006). TPR at fixed FPR needs enough negatives for the FPR to be measured: estimating a 1% FPR within about 0.2 points takes roughly 10,000 negatives.

Several of these metrics are algebraic relatives. F1 = 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN), the harmonic mean of precision and recall; it never mentions TN, so it ignores how many negatives you correctly passed. Fβ = (1+β²)PR/(β²P+R). MCC = (TP·TN - FP·FN)/√((TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN)) is the Pearson correlation between the binary prediction and truth, and is symmetric under swapping the roles of the classes, unlike F1.

Precision is the metric that moves with prevalence π. By Bayes' rule, precision = TPR·π / (TPR·π + FPR·(1-π)); recall and FPR are properties of the classifier given class-conditional score distributions, but precision also depends on how common positives are. A model with 90% recall and 5% FPR has precision 95% at 50% prevalence but only about 15% at 1% prevalence.

If class-conditional score distributions stay the same at deployment, TPR and FPR carry over but precision does not when prevalence differs, which is why TPR at a fixed FPR is the shippable number.

Calibration answers a different question: when the score says 0.3, do roughly 30% of such cases turn out positive? Expected calibration error bins predictions by confidence and averages the gap between mean confidence and observed frequency, weighted by bin size; it is sensitive to binning, so a reliability plot is more honest. If the score is calibrated and you know the costs, the optimal threshold is t = C_FP/(C_FP + C_FN): when a miss is nine times costlier than a false alarm, flag anything above 0.1.

Check the arithmetic in Trap 1: always predicting negative gives 9,990/10,000 = 99.9% accuracy, precision undefined (0/0), and recall 0. Also note the reverse degenerate classifier: flag everything and recall is 100%, with precision equal to the prevalence. Any single number can be gamed by moving along the threshold, so report the curve or a stated operating point.

Trap 2 compounds with small samples. If the test set holds 10 positives, one more detection moves recall by ten points, and the exact 95% confidence interval for 7 caught out of 10 spans roughly 35% to 93%. Choosing the F1-maximizing threshold on the test set then reports the best of many looks; the threshold must be fixed on validation data before the test set is scored. Report the threshold, its selection rule, the number of positives, and an interval.
ml-metrics-01.further: Misconceptions: AUROC is not accuracy at the best threshold, a high AUROC does not mean probabilities are trustworthy, and a high AUPRC on one dataset cannot be compared with a lower one on another with different prevalence. For probes and classifiers inside language-model research (the framing of this page), prefer AUROC for comparing representations and TPR at a fixed FPR for deployment decisions. Gotchas: ties in scores, sampling negatives (which changes precision and the PR baseline but not ROC), and averaging metrics across classes (macro versus micro) hide different failures. The next page applies these metrics to heavily imbalanced data, and the debugging page treats a suspiciously high score as a leak until proven otherwise.

The majority-class baseline scores 1 - π accuracy where π is prevalence, so at π = 1% a model must beat 99% to do anything. A classifier that outputs the base rate for every input is perfectly calibrated and has zero discriminative power.

Imbalance itself is not the main problem; the number of positives is. Estimation error for recall scales with 1/√(n_positive), so a dataset of a million rows with 50 positives is effectively a dataset of 50 for anything positive-related. That is why the toy example (10 positives in 1,000) is fragile: swapping two predictions changes recall by 20 points. Logistic regression also underestimates event probabilities when events are very rare (King and Zeng 2001).

Under imbalance the loss is dominated by negatives: the cheapest way to lower average cross-entropy early is to push every output toward the base rate. A common remedy is to initialize the final bias to the log-odds of the prior, log(π/(1-π)), so training starts calibrated to prevalence rather than wasting steps learning it (the RetinaNet paper uses a related prior initialization).

Calibration drifts mostly because of what you do about imbalance. If you oversample, undersample, or reweight, the model learns probabilities for the altered class mix. Correction is a shift in log-odds: for a model trained with negatives subsampled by a factor, the output odds must be rescaled by that factor (Elkan 2001). Forgetting this gives scores that rank well but whose absolute values, and therefore any probability threshold, are wrong by a large factor.

Link the metrics through the confusion matrix. Precision = TP/(TP+FP), recall = TP/(TP+FN), F1 = 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN) (identical to the Dice coefficient). Balanced accuracy is macro-averaged recall, so it equals 0.5 for any constant predictor, unlike plain accuracy.

ROC-AUC is insensitive to prevalence by construction, which sounds like a virtue but means it can look strong while precision is poor. Saito and Rehmsmeier (2015) demonstrated this with simulations and recommended PR plots for imbalanced data. Remember, though, that a PR curve's baseline is the prevalence, so a PR-AUC of 0.30 can be excellent at 1% prevalence and poor at 40%. Normalize a confusion matrix by row (true class) to read recall, by column (predicted class) to read precision.

Resampling before splitting puts copies or near-copies of training points into validation. Do resampling inside each training fold (imbalanced-learn's Pipeline does this); never touch validation or test data, which must keep the real class mix.

SMOTE (Chawla et al. 2002) creates a synthetic point by choosing a minority example x, one of its k nearest minority neighbors x', and sampling x + u(x' - x) with u uniform in [0,1]. It assumes straight lines between minority points stay in minority territory, which fails with categorical features, high dimensions, class overlap and multimodal minorities, where it generates plausible-looking but wrong points. For strong learners such as gradient-boosted trees, practitioners often find class weights and threshold tuning perform as well; test it rather than assuming it helps.

Class weighting multiplies each example's loss; weights inverse to class frequency (n/(2·n_k) in scikit-learn's "balanced") shift the decision boundary in the same way oversampling does, but without duplicating data. Focal loss (Lin et al. 2017, introduced with RetinaNet) is FL = -α(1-p_t)^γ log(p_t), where p_t is the probability assigned to the true class: the (1-p_t)^γ factor shrinks the contribution of easy, confidently correct examples (γ = 2 was their default), so the many easy negatives stop swamping the gradient.

For a calibrated model, moving the threshold is theoretically equivalent to reweighting costs, and Elkan (2001) argued that thresholding is often the simplest correct tool. One-class methods (one-class SVM, Isolation Forest of Liu et al. 2008, autoencoder reconstruction error) model normal data and flag outliers; they assume anomalies look different, not just rarer.

Match the objective to how the system is used. If a human reviews a fixed number of cases, use precision at k (precision among the top k scored items) or TPR at the implied FPR, not a global AUC. If the cost of a miss and of a false alarm are known, minimize expected cost C_FN·FN + C_FP·FP over thresholds and plot cost against threshold: the minimum is your operating point, and its flatness shows how sensitive the choice is. PR-AUC averages over all operating points, including ones you will never use; consider partial AUC or the deployed point.

Also check that prevalence is stable. If positives become more common in production, the precision at a fixed threshold rises without any model change; if the case mix changes, recall may fall.

Some steps hide sub-decisions. Calibration: Platt scaling fits a logistic function (two parameters) to the scores, suited to small calibration sets; isotonic regression fits a free-form monotone step function and needs more data (roughly over a thousand calibration examples is a common guideline) or it overfits (Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana 2005). Calibrate and choose thresholds on data the model did not train on, and keep these two uses separate when positives are few, or use cross-validated predictions.

For uncertainty, a stratified bootstrap (resample positives and negatives separately) gives confidence intervals on recall, precision and AUPRC. For error analysis, slice false negatives and false positives by data source, time, length, subgroup and label confidence, since rare-class errors often cluster in one slice or in mislabeled examples.

The balanced-test-set trap can be computed. Take TPR = 90% and FPR = 5%. On a 50/50 test set, precision = 0.9·0.5 / (0.9·0.5 + 0.05·0.5) = 94.7%. At 1% prevalence, precision = 0.9·0.01 / (0.9·0.01 + 0.05·0.99) = 0.009/0.0585, about 15%: five out of six alerts are false. A balanced test set is fine for ranking models, but any precision, F1 or PPV claim must be recomputed at deployment prevalence using TPR and FPR.

On "perfect score on tiny support": getting 3 of 3 positives right still leaves a 95% lower bound for recall of only about 37% (0.05^(1/3)). Subgroup failures hide inside averages, so compute metrics per slice with intervals; a model can be fine overall and poor for a group that has few positives. Drift changes prevalence, features and labels, so monitor all three.

Turn the checklist numbers into requirements. To estimate recall near 0.8 with a ±5-point 95% interval you need about 1.96²·0.8·0.2/0.05² ≈ 250 positives in the evaluation set. To measure an FPR near 1% within ±0.2 points takes about 9,500 negatives. If you cannot get these counts, say so and widen the claimed uncertainty instead of reporting a point estimate. The positives you have also have to be representative: positives found by an existing system (for example, only items a previous rule flagged) bias the set toward cases that system already catches, and labeling only flagged items hides the false negatives entirely. A cheap remedy is to label a random sample of unflagged items to estimate the miss rate, then weight by sampling fraction.
ml-metrics-02.further: Misconceptions: imbalance does not automatically require resampling, 0.5 is not a natural threshold, and a higher PR-AUC from a rebalanced test set is not progress. In many cases the best sequence is a strong baseline, class weights or none, calibrated probabilities, then a threshold derived from costs or a review budget. Gotchas: label noise hurts the minority class most, because a handful of mislabeled positives is a large fraction of the class; and monitoring in production needs delayed labels, so build a labeled sampling stream early. This page builds on the classification-metrics and cross-validation pages (stratified and grouped folds), and its final checklist doubles as a leakage audit for the debugging page.

In the potential-outcomes framework (Rubin), each unit has two outcomes, Y(1) if treated and Y(0) if not, and the causal effect is their difference. Only one is observed: the fundamental problem of causal inference. The average treatment effect is E[Y(1) - Y(0)]. The observed difference between treated and untreated groups equals the ATE plus a selection-bias term whenever those groups would have differed even without treatment; randomization sets that term to zero in expectation.

Pearl's notation separates seeing from doing: P(y | x) is what you observe when X happens to be x, while P(y | do(x)) is what happens when you set X to x. Correlation (usually Pearson r) measures only linear association; y = x² on symmetric x has r = 0 despite perfect dependence. Prediction needs only the first; decisions need the second.

Draw the three basic causal shapes. A fork (Z causes X and Y) is confounding: X and Y correlate, and conditioning on Z removes the spurious part. A chain (X causes M causes Y) is mediation: controlling for M blocks a real effect. A collider (X and Y both cause C) is the reverse: X and Y are independent until you condition on C, which creates a spurious association. This is Berkson's paradox (1946), the mechanism behind "only look at admitted patients".

Simpson's paradox shows aggregation can reverse a trend: the 1973 UC Berkeley admissions data (Bickel et al. 1975) showed lower overall acceptance for women while most departments showed no disadvantage, because women applied more to harder departments. Two trending series correlate strongly even if unrelated (Granger and Newbold 1974), so detrend first.

Randomization balances confounders in expectation, including ones you never measured, but it needs care. Assignment must be truly random and independent of outcomes; check for sample ratio mismatch (observed group sizes deviating from the planned split). Interference matters too: in a marketplace or social network, treating one unit changes outcomes of others, violating the usual no-interference assumption.

Without randomization, each tool buys identification with an assumption. Adjustment needs all confounders measured (the backdoor criterion: block every non-causal path). Propensity scores (Rosenbaum and Rubin 1983) balance observed covariates only. Difference-in-differences assumes parallel trends absent treatment. Instrumental variables need an instrument that affects outcome only via treatment. None of these is testable fully, hence sensitivity analyses such as the E-value (VanderWeele and Ding 2017): how strong would an unmeasured confounder have to be?

Pearl describes a ladder: association (seeing), intervention (doing), counterfactual (imagining). Each rung needs assumptions the lower rung's data cannot supply. A modern formalization is target trial emulation (Hernán and Robins 2016): when analyzing observational data, write down the randomized trial you wish you had (eligibility, treatment strategies, start time, outcome, analysis) and make the data mimic it.

Wording matters because it signals the design. "Predicts" and "is associated with" are fine for correlational evidence. A subtle ML point: a feature that is highly predictive of the outcome (or has high attribution in an explainer) is not necessarily a lever. Emergency room visits predict illness, but reducing visits will not reduce illness.

A correlation of R = 0.92 gives R² = 0.85, meaning 85% of variance is shared linearly, and still says nothing about direction, confounding, or whether the relation is stable under intervention. Searching over many variables will always find striking correlations by chance; with 1,000 candidate series, thousands of pairs will clear a nominal threshold.

Statistical significance also depends on sample size: with n = 10,000, a correlation of just 0.02 gives p of about 0.046, yet explains 0.04% of variance.

For product decisions, a standard trap is self-selection: users who adopt a feature retain better, but engaged users are the ones who adopt it. A churn model predicts who leaves, not whom a discount would retain; for that you need uplift modeling or a randomized holdout.

Make the checklist operational. Negative-control outcomes (outcomes the treatment cannot plausibly affect) and placebo tests (a fake treatment date, a fake population) reveal hidden bias: if the "effect" appears where none can exist, your design is picking up confounding. Check dose-response (does more exposure produce more effect?) and consistency across settings and methods. The Bradford Hill considerations (1965), such as strength, consistency, temporality, dose-response and plausibility, remain a useful informal list, with temporality the only strictly necessary item.

Also write the causal diagram before modeling and ask which arrows you are assuming absent; each missing arrow is a claim. Report how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be to nullify the result. Finally, distinguish robustness of the estimate (stable under analysis choices) from validity (correct under the real world), because a stable biased estimate is still biased.
ml-research-02.further: Misconceptions: controlling for more variables is not always better (colliders and mediators), randomization does not guarantee balance in every sample, and causal inference is not only for experiments; it is a framework for stating assumptions explicitly. In ML practice, the topic returns constantly: spurious features that predict in training but fail under shift (shortcut learning), evaluating a recommender or LLM feature by A/B test, and interpretability findings that are correlational unless you intervene on activations. The interpretability page shows that causal-intervention experiments (patching) are exactly the do() operation applied to a network. Use this page's wording discipline in everything you write.

Treat red flags as a prior: most genuine improvements are small, so a big jump deserves proportional scrutiny. Near-perfect scores usually mean leakage, a trivial task, or train-test overlap. Worse-than-random is informative too: an AUROC of 0.2 means the signal is real but inverted, often a flipped label or sign, rather than a model failure.

High variance across seeds is a measurement problem: if run-to-run standard deviation is comparable to the gap between methods, the gap is not established. Report mean and spread over several seeds (Henderson et al. 2018 documented how fragile deep RL comparisons are to seeds and codebase details). Loss curves have fingerprints: a plateau at ln(K) means the model outputs the uniform distribution (not learning); rising loss often points to a too-high learning rate; a validation curve that diverges while training improves is overfitting.

Practice "becoming one with the data" (Karpathy's phrase): read raw examples, look at extremes, count, and plot. Check units and ranges (meters versus feet, seconds versus milliseconds), dtypes, and that the target definition matches what you think. Missingness is not neutral: whether a value is missing can itself predict the label (for example a lab test is only ordered for sicker patients), leaking information through a pattern rather than a value.

A powerful systematic check is adversarial validation: train a classifier to distinguish train rows from test rows; an AUROC far above 0.5 means the distributions differ and shows which features differ. Label noise matters too: Northcutt et al. (2021) estimated that widely used benchmark test sets contain a few percent label errors, enough to change model rankings. Deduplicate by hashing.

Variance inflation factor: VIF_j = 1/(1 - R²_j), where R²_j comes from regressing feature j on all other features. A VIF of 5 means R² = 0.8; a VIF of 10 means R² = 0.9. The condition number is the ratio of largest to smallest singular value of the (standardized) design matrix; thresholds are conventions.

What collinearity damages matters: it inflates the standard errors and makes individual coefficients unstable and uninterpretable (sign flips between runs), but if the correlation structure persists at test time, predictions may stay fine. So it is mainly an interpretation problem. Ridge regression stabilizes by shrinking along low-variance directions; lasso tends to pick one of a correlated group arbitrarily. Polynomial and interaction terms create collinearity by construction, so center variables before forming them.

Leakage has recognizable families (Kaufman et al. 2012): target information in a feature (a field created after the outcome, like "discharge code" when predicting readmission); preprocessing fit on all data (scaling, target encoding, imputation, feature selection); temporal leakage (random splits on time-ordered data); and duplicate or group overlap. The Clever Hans phenomenon is a related failure: a model uses a spurious cue. In medical imaging, Zech et al. (2018) showed pneumonia classifiers partly keyed on hospital-specific signals rather than disease, and did significantly worse on other hospitals' data in 3 of 5 comparisons. Kapoor and Narayanan (2023) surveyed leakage across ML-based science, finding it widespread.

Detection tactics: train single-feature models and see which feature alone scores suspiciously high; inspect the top feature importances for things that should not be knowable at prediction time; and rerun with a time-based or group-based split to see whether performance collapses.

If scores are unexpectedly bad, bisect: shrink to a tiny dataset and verify the model can memorize it; if not, the bug is in code, loss, optimizer or labels. Shuffle the labels as a test: performance should fall to chance, and if it does not, evaluation is leaking. A classic bug: shuffling X and y independently. Check that preprocessing at inference matches training (tokenizer version, normalization statistics, image resize), and that the model is in eval mode (dropout off, batch-norm running statistics on).

Then consider distribution shift, which has distinct flavors: covariate shift (inputs change, relationship same), label or prior shift (class frequencies change), and concept drift (the relationship itself changes). Name which you suspect and test it, e.g. by checking performance by time slice.

Two curve types get called learning curves: loss versus training steps, and performance versus training set size. The second is the classic bias-variance diagnostic: high-bias models plateau high with train and validation close, so more data will not help, you need capacity or better features; high-variance models show a gap that narrows with more data.

This picture needs care for modern deep networks. Double descent (Belkin et al. 2019; Nakkiran et al. 2019) shows test error can be non-monotone in model size or training time: it can peak near the point where the model just fits the training data and then fall again. A train-validation gap alone is therefore not proof you should shrink the model; judge by validation performance.

Residual plots expose model misspecification: a curve suggests missing nonlinearity, a funnel shape (variance growing with the fitted value) means heteroscedasticity, which breaks standard errors but not necessarily point predictions. The QQ plot compares residual quantiles against a normal distribution; it matters for small-sample inference, less for prediction; heavy tails bend the ends away from the line.

The IQR rule flags points outside Q1 - 1.5·IQR and Q3 + 1.5·IQR, but an outlier is a question, not a verdict: it may be an error or the most important case. SHAP (Lundberg and Lee 2017) assigns each feature a Shapley-value contribution to a prediction. Remember its limits: it explains the model, not the world, correlated features share credit unpredictably. A sensible importance ranking is a necessary sanity check, not proof of correctness.

Reproducibility is step one because a result you cannot reproduce cannot be debugged. Fix seeds for Python, NumPy and the framework; know that some GPU operations (for example those using atomic additions) are nondeterministic unless you request deterministic algorithms, so exact bit-equality may be impossible and seed-to-seed variance must be measured instead. Log code version, data version, and configuration with each run.

Baselines should include trivial ones (majority class, previous value, mean) and strong simple ones (linear model, gradient-boosted trees) tuned fairly. Ablate your own contribution: remove the new component and confirm the gain disappears. Stress testing means rerunning under different seeds, different splits (especially group- or time-based), perturbed inputs, and different data subsets, and checking that the conclusion holds. Interpretation closes the loop with error analysis: read actual failures, because a model can be right for the wrong reasons.

The final checklist question, "would I bet money?", is a Bayesian prompt: weigh how surprising the result is against how reliable your process is. Twyman's law says any figure that looks interesting or different is usually wrong; a surprising result is more often a bug than a discovery, so the burden of proof scales with surprise. Practical tools include an independent reimplementation of the evaluation, a locked test set touched once, a canary evaluation on fresh data, and a pre-mortem (imagine the result later turned out wrong and write down why).

Being unable to tick a box is information, not failure: record it as a known limitation in the write-up. Prefer reporting a modest claim with evidence over a bold one without it; reviewers and users alike eventually test the bold one.

Each mental model has a technical form. Garbage in, garbage out: if a fraction η of test labels are wrong, even a perfect model is capped near 1 - η measured accuracy, and noisy training labels bias fits. Occam's razor appears as regularization and as the minimum description length idea (prefer the model that compresses data best); it is a preference, not a guarantee, and the no-free-lunch theorems (Wolpert 1996) say no learner wins on all problems without assumptions.

Seeking disconfirming evidence is Popper's falsification applied to everyday work: design the test that would embarrass your hypothesis. Documenting everything has a modern form: an experiment tracker recording config, data hash, code commit, and metrics, so every number in a table has provenance. Being humble is quantifiable: report intervals and log what you tried.
ml-research-03.further: Misconceptions: a red flag is not proof of a bug (some tasks really are easy, some gains real), and passing a checklist does not prove correctness; the checks reduce the odds of common errors. Gotchas: debugging by changing several things at once, trusting a single seed, and tuning on the metric you later report. This page connects every earlier foundation page: leakage and splits (cross-validation), metrics on rare classes (classification and imbalance pages), the association-versus-cause caution (previous page) and training pathologies (deep-learning basics). Later pages on evaluating language models reuse the same suspicion, with extra concerns such as benchmark contamination and judge bias.

The twelve chapters trace one object through its life. A transformer is defined (architecture), run (serving), shaped (post-training and alignment), judged (evals), planned (scaling laws), opened up (interpretability), constrained (safety), built at scale (distributed training and tokenization), and finally wrapped into products (agents, fine-tuning versus retrieval, system design). Each stage constrains the others: the vocabulary chosen at tokenization fixes the embedding matrix size and sequence lengths; the attention design fixes KV-cache cost, which fixes serving economics; evaluation choices decide what post-training actually optimizes.

The blueprint shown is the original encoder-decoder transformer (Vaswani et al. 2017). Most current LLMs keep only the decoder stack with causal self-attention and no cross-attention. A good habit throughout the guide: for any claim, ask what tensor shapes are involved, what is the bottleneck (compute, memory bandwidth, communication, data), and what you would measure to check.
ml-llm-internals-01.further: How to use this guide: the chapters are ordered so each depends on earlier ones. Transformer shapes feed serving memory math; serving math reappears in system design; evaluation methodology underlies both alignment and scaling claims. Expect interview-style questions to chain chapters, for example "why does long context hurt serving cost?" needs attention, KV cache, memory bandwidth and batching in one answer. Gotcha: many numbers quoted in industry (throughputs, prices, utilization) change quickly; the durable skill is deriving them from first principles with stated assumptions. Where practice is unsettled, such as the best alignment algorithm or how to read emergent abilities, the later pages say so rather than pretending there is consensus.

panels: Why divide by √d_head? If query and key entries have zero mean and unit variance, a dot product over d_head terms has variance d_head, so scores grow with head size and softmax saturates into near one-hot, giving tiny gradients. Dividing by √d_head restores unit variance. The full cost matters: the score and weighted-sum matmuls take about O(B·h·T²·d_head) FLOPs, and the [B, h, T, T] tensor is quadratic in sequence length, which is why long context is expensive in both memory and compute. FlashAttention (Dao et al. 2022) computes exactly the same result in tiles using an online softmax, never writing the full T×T matrix to GPU main memory, so it is faster mainly by cutting memory traffic, not FLOPs.

Concatenating heads and applying W_O lets later layers mix information found by different heads. Heads often specialize (previous-token, induction, syntax-like patterns), but not uniformly: Michel et al. (2019) found many heads can be pruned at test time with little loss, so head count is not a measure of capability.

The causal mask is implemented by adding minus infinity to the scores above the diagonal before softmax, making those weights exactly zero. Two subtleties: in half precision, a fully masked row (for example a padded query position) yields NaN unless handled, and the mask also means that during training all T positions give a next-token loss in one forward pass. That is the efficiency that makes autoregressive pretraining cheap compared with generation.

The point of GQA and MQA is the KV cache, not FLOPs. Cache size per token per layer is 2 × H_kv × d_head values, so cutting KV heads from h to g shrinks the cache by h/g, which both allows larger batches and reduces the bytes read per decode step (decode is memory-bandwidth bound). Multi-query attention (Shazeer 2019) shares one K/V head across all queries; grouped-query attention (Ainslie et al. 2023) interpolates, and they showed an MHA checkpoint can be converted by averaging K/V heads within groups and briefly continuing training.

A newer alternative is multi-head latent attention (DeepSeek-V2, 2024), which caches a compressed latent vector and reconstructs K and V from it.

Without a cache, generating token T+1 would recompute K and V for all T earlier tokens at every layer, making total work over a generation O(T²) in projections. With the cache, each step computes one new row of Q, K, V per layer and attends over the stored keys: per-step attention cost is O(T·d) rather than O(T²·d). Note that decode remains expensive: each step still streams all model weights and the whole cache from memory, so it is bandwidth-bound.

Cache memory is the practical limit on concurrency. Naive contiguous allocation wastes memory through fragmentation and over-reservation for maximum length; PagedAttention (Kwon et al. 2023, vLLM) stores the cache in fixed-size blocks mapped through a table, like virtual memory, and enables sharing of common prefixes between requests.

RoPE (Su et al. 2021) treats each pair of dimensions in a query or key as a 2D vector and rotates it by an angle p·θ_i, where p is the position and θ_i = base^(-2i/d) with base commonly 10,000, giving a spread of frequencies. Because rotations compose, the dot product between a rotated query at position m and key at position n depends only on m - n, so attention sees relative offsets even though absolute positions were used to rotate.

Beyond training length, high-frequency components see angles never encountered in training, and quality degrades. Extensions rescale positions or frequencies: position interpolation (Chen et al. 2023) compresses positions into the trained range, and NTK-aware and YaRN variants (Peng et al. 2023) scale frequencies non-uniformly; each usually needs some fine-tuning.

The practical difference is where the norm sits relative to the residual path. In post-norm, x_{l+1} = LN(x_l + F(x_l)), so every layer's output passes through a norm and the identity path is not clean; at initialization the gradient scale near the output is large, which is why post-norm needed learning-rate warmup and was fragile at depth (Xiong et al. 2020 analyzed this). In pre-norm, x_{l+1} = x_l + F(LN(x_l)), so the residual stream is an uninterrupted sum and gradients flow directly. Pre-norm typically needs a final norm before the output head, and the stream's norm tends to grow with depth, which can make later layers' contributions relatively smaller.

Most recent LLMs use pre-norm with RMSNorm (Zhang and Sennrich 2019), which drops mean-centering and rescales by the root mean square only, saving compute with similar quality.

Think of the residual stream as a shared bus of width d_model. Each attention head and MLP reads from it (after normalization), computes something, and writes an additive update back. This view, developed in the mathematical framework for transformer circuits (Elhage et al. 2021), explains several facts: layers can communicate across arbitrary depth without intermediate layers needing to relay information; the gradient has an identity path (the derivative of x_L with respect to x_l includes an identity term), which is why very deep stacks train; and the final residual vector is simply unembedded into logits.

The stream's width is a bottleneck: all information passing between layers must fit in d_model dimensions, so features are stored in superposition (more features than dimensions).

Reasoning through the drill: given B, T, d_model, h, d_head = d_model/h. Storing scores costs B·h·T² elements, which at B=8, h=32, T=8192 in bf16 is 8·32·67M·2 bytes, about 34 GB per layer if materialized, which is exactly why fused kernels exist. A stable softmax subtracts the row maximum before exponentiating; softmax is shift-invariant, so the answer is unchanged, but exp can no longer overflow.

For the mask, the code adds a matrix with minus infinity above the diagonal and zero elsewhere. Common follow-ups: how does the mask change for padding or prefix-LM (bidirectional attention over a prefix)? What changes at decode time (the new query attends to every cached key, so no mask is needed)?
ml-llm-internals-03.further: Misconceptions: attention weights are not a faithful explanation of model behavior (a high weight does not mean that token determines the output), the softmax is over keys for each query rather than over queries, and positions are not "added" in RoPE-based models, they are applied inside attention. Gotchas: tensor layout conventions differ between libraries ([B, T, h, d] versus [B, h, T, d]), and bugs often hide in transposes. Connections: the KV cache and GQA here set the memory math on the serving page; the residual stream is the object studied on the interpretability page; pre-norm, RMSNorm and learning-rate warmup connect to the training-stability issues in distributed training.

The formula is right: bytes = 2 × L × B × T × H_kv × d_head × bytes per element. Worked example: with L=80, B=8, T=4096, H_kv=8, d_head=128 and 2 bytes, the product is 10,737,418,240 bytes, which is 10 GiB (about 10.7 GB). A quick check is per token: 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 327,680 bytes, about 320 KiB per token, times 8 × 4096 = 32,768 cached tokens.

The structure to remember: cache size is linear in batch, in context length, in layer count, and in KV heads, which is why GQA matters.

The split follows arithmetic intensity, FLOPs per byte moved. In prefill, the weights are reused across all T prompt tokens, so each loaded weight does many multiply-adds: compute-bound. In decode with batch B, each step loads all weights (2N bytes in bf16) to do about 2·N·B FLOPs, an intensity of roughly B FLOPs per byte. A modern accelerator needs a few hundred FLOPs per byte to saturate its compute (H100 SXM: about 990 TFLOPs dense bf16 over about 3.35 TB/s is roughly 300), so decode at small batch is far below that line and runs at memory bandwidth. A useful bound: decode time per token is at least weight bytes divided by bandwidth, so a 70B bf16 model (140 GB) needs about 42 ms per step on a single 3.35 TB/s device, less when sharded across devices.

TTFT contains queueing delay, tokenization, network, and the prefill itself; prefill time grows at least linearly with prompt length, and the attention part grows quadratically, so long prompts can dominate TTFT. TPOT depends on batch size, context length (cache reads) and the decode kernel efficiency, and rises as the server packs more concurrent requests. Check the example: 1.250 + 200 × 0.045 = 10.25 s, confirming that for long outputs TPOT is nearly everything (9 s of 10.25 s).

Production metrics need distributions, not averages: report p50 and p99 TTFT and TPOT, because tail latency drives user experience and SLOs. Streaming means TPOT should stay below reading speed.

With static batching, a batch runs until its longest sequence finishes, so short requests wait and slots sit idle. Continuous (iteration-level) batching, introduced by Orca (Yu et al. 2022), makes the scheduling decision at every decode step: finished sequences leave immediately and waiting requests join, so the GPU runs a full batch nearly all the time. It depends on the cache being flexibly allocated, which is why it pairs naturally with paged memory.

The subtle issue is interference. A new request's prefill is a large compute burst that delays the decode steps of everyone already running (head-of-line blocking), inflating their TPOT. Chunked prefill splits long prompts into pieces interleaved with decode steps to smooth this. Admission, preemption and priority policies determine tail latency.

Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al. 2023; Chen et al. 2023) is lossless. The draft model with distribution q proposes k tokens; the target model with distribution p scores all k positions in one forward pass. Each proposed token x is accepted with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)); at the first rejection, a replacement is sampled from the normalized positive part of (p - q), and the rest are discarded.

Expected tokens per target call, with per-token acceptance rate α treated as constant, is (1 - α^(k+1))/(1 - α); for α = 0.8 and k = 4 that is about 3.4. The gain exists because decode is bandwidth-bound, so verifying several tokens costs about as much as generating one. At large batch sizes, decode becomes compute-bound, the extra verification FLOPs are no longer free, and the benefit shrinks.

Distinguish what is quantized. Weight-only schemes (such as 4-bit AWQ or GPTQ) reduce bytes read per decode step, which directly speeds up the bandwidth-bound decode phase, but compute still happens in 16-bit after dequantization. Weight-and-activation schemes (INT8 W8A8, FP8) also use low-precision tensor cores, helping compute-bound prefill and large batches. Activation outliers in LLMs make W8A8 hard (Dettmers et al. 2022, LLM.int8()); AWQ (Lin et al. 2023) protects the small fraction of weight channels that matter most, identified by activation magnitude, by scaling them before rounding.

FP8 comes in two layouts: E4M3 (more mantissa, max about 448) for tensors, E5M2 (more range) for gradients. AWQ's compression ratio depends on bit-width and group-scale overhead (a 4-bit group-128 scheme is about 4.25 bits per weight), not on sparsity.

Treat this as a queueing-and-roofline problem. Per-token cost = (GPU price per hour × GPUs) / (tokens per hour). Raising the batch size increases throughput almost for free while decode is bandwidth-bound (weights are read once for many sequences) until the step becomes compute-bound or the cache fills memory; beyond that, latency rises linearly with no throughput gain. In queueing terms, waiting time blows up as utilization approaches 100% (for a simple M/M/1 queue it scales like ρ/(1-ρ)), so running servers hot saves money but wrecks tail latency; leaving headroom is a cost.

Parallelism choices map onto the triangle. Tensor parallelism splits each layer over GPUs, lowering per-token latency (aggregate bandwidth) but adding all-reduce communication; replicas multiply throughput without helping single-request latency.

Interview napkin math should include a sanity pass. Weights: 70B × 2 bytes = 140 GB, which exceeds a single 80 GB GPU, so at least two are needed for weights alone and in practice four or more once you leave room for cache. For the panel's cache configuration, the per-token figure is 327,680 bytes (320 KiB), so for batch 8 the total is about 10 GiB at 4K tokens, 80 GiB at 32K, 320 GiB at 128K and 640 GiB at 256K, scaling linearly with context. By 32K tokens at batch 8, the cache already rivals the 140 GB of weights.

Distinguish GB from GiB (a 7% gap) and leave room for activations and fragmentation.
ml-llm-production-02.further: Misconceptions: more GPUs do not always reduce latency (communication overhead), quantization is not free quality-wise (always evaluate on your task, especially long context and reasoning). Gotchas: benchmark numbers depend on prompt and output length distributions, so test with realistic traffic; cost per token depends heavily on utilization, so an idle fleet is the dominant cost in practice. This page builds on the transformer page (GQA, cache), and its tradeoffs reappear in system design, where TTFT, TPOT, caching and batching become requirements.

panels:
Each stage changes what the model is optimized for. Pretraining minimizes next-token cross-entropy over trillions of tokens and produces a model that continues text, not one that follows instructions. Post-training is much cheaper in tokens, and a surprising amount of conversational behavior comes from small, carefully curated data: the LIMA study (Zhou et al. 2023) reached strong chat quality with about 1,000 curated examples, motivating the "superficial alignment" hypothesis that most knowledge is learned in pretraining and post-training mainly teaches style and format.

Since 2024, a major additional branch is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (math answers checked, code run against tests), as in DeepSeek-R1 (2025) using GRPO (a PPO variant without a value network), which replaces the learned reward model with programmatic checks wherever one exists.

Mechanically, SFT is next-token cross-entropy on (prompt, response) pairs formatted with a chat template, with the loss usually computed only on response tokens (prompt tokens are masked). Because it only imitates, its ceiling is the demonstrators: it cannot teach the model to be better than the examples, and it penalizes any valid answer that differs from the reference wording.

A subtle failure: if demonstrations contain facts the base model does not know, SFT can teach it to produce confident-sounding claims anyway, which is one proposed source of hallucination; Gekhman et al. (2024) reported that fine-tuning on unknown facts is learned slowly and increases hallucination, though conclusions depend on setup. SFT is also the reference policy for later KL penalties, so a weak SFT model limits everything downstream.

The reward model is typically the SFT language model with its output head replaced by a scalar head read at the final token. Training minimizes -log σ(r(x, y_w) - r(x, y_l)), where y_w is the preferred response: this is the Bradley-Terry model (1952), which implies P(A ≻ B) = σ(r(A) - r(B)), the same as the panel's ratio of exponentials. Only reward differences are identified, so the reward is usually normalized before RL.

The reward model is a lossy proxy for human preference. Known artifacts include a preference for longer responses (length bias), for confident or flattering tone, and sensitivity to position and formatting. Sharma et al. (2023) showed that preference data and trained preference models can reward agreeing with the user's stated views, one root of sycophancy.

Structure of the objective: the per-token KL penalty is folded into the reward, and the KL-regularized problem has a closed-form optimum, π*(y|x) ∝ π_ref(y|x) · exp(r(x, y)/β). PPO (Schulman et al. 2017) optimizes this with a clipped surrogate, min(ρ·A, clip(ρ, 1-ε, 1+ε)·A), where ρ is the new-to-old probability ratio and A the advantage estimated with a learned value function. In memory this means up to four models: policy, reference, reward model and value network, which is why PPO RLHF is expensive and finicky.

Reward hacking is quantifiable: Gao et al. (2023) showed that as the policy drifts further (in KL) from the reference, the proxy reward keeps rising while a held-out "gold" reward eventually falls. Monitor KL, response length and fresh independent evaluation, not just training reward.

The panel's formula is the intuition; the actual DPO loss (Rafailov et al. 2023) is -log σ(β [log(π_θ(y⁺|x)/π_ref(y⁺|x)) - log(π_θ(y⁻|x)/π_ref(y⁻|x))]). It comes from rearranging the KL-regularized optimum to write the reward as r = β log(π_θ/π_ref) + a prompt-dependent constant, then substituting into the Bradley-Terry likelihood, where the constant cancels. So DPO is a classification loss on an implicit reward with KL control built in; larger β holds the policy closer to the reference.

Because it trains on a fixed dataset of pairs, DPO is offline: responses were generated by some other model, so there is a distribution mismatch with the current policy. Documented quirks include both chosen and rejected likelihoods decreasing during training, and a tendency to lengthen responses. Whether online PPO-style RL or DPO is better remains unsettled and depends on data, tuning effort and task.

RLAIF replaces human labelers with a model that applies a rubric. Evidence is encouraging but conditional: Lee et al. (2023) found AI-feedback RL comparable to human-feedback RL on summarization and helpfulness tasks, and Constitutional AI (Bai et al. 2022) used AI labels for harmlessness. The key risk is correlated error: the judge's blind spots (including the biases in the evaluation chapter, such as position and length bias) get amplified, since the policy is optimized against them.

Design defenses: write explicit rubrics with examples; ask for a critique before the verdict; randomize presentation order; use a judge stronger than or independent of the policy; and validate the judge against a human-labeled sample by measuring agreement per category, since overall agreement hides weak slices. Keep human evaluation as the final audit; any fixed AI judge will eventually be exploited.

Constitutional AI (Bai et al. 2022) has two stages. In the supervised stage, the model answers red-team prompts, then critiques its own answer against a randomly drawn principle and writes a revision; the revised responses become SFT data. In the RL stage, an AI labeler chooses which of two responses better satisfies a principle (often with a chain-of-thought rationale), those AI preferences train a preference model for harmlessness (combined with human preferences for helpfulness), and the policy is optimized against it.

The advantage is transparency and scalability: behavior is steered by readable text that can be audited and edited. Limits: the principles are only as good as the model's ability to interpret and apply them, vague principles conflict, and who writes the constitution is a governance question.

Choosing among methods is mostly a question of what feedback you have. SFT needs demonstrations. DPO needs pairs and is the cheapest way to use them, so it is a common baseline. PPO-style RL needs a reward signal that can score fresh samples (a learned reward model, or a programmatic verifier), and its on-policy exploration can find behaviors absent from any dataset, which is why it dominates for tasks with checkable answers.

None solves the underlying problem that the training signal is a proxy. Failure modes to name: reward hacking (the policy exploits proxy flaws), mode collapse and reduced output diversity (sometimes called the alignment tax), sycophancy, over-refusal from over-weighted safety data, and verbosity. Evaluate with win-rate against a baseline alongside KL or length, and hold out data from the preference distribution.
ml-llm-internals-06.further: Misconceptions: RLHF does not teach new knowledge so much as steer existing capability; alignment is not a one-time stage but a loop of data, optimization and evaluation; and the KL penalty is not a safety guarantee, only a trust region around the reference. DPO is not RL, though it optimizes the same regularized objective in closed form. Gotchas: preference data quality dominates algorithm choice; always compare against a strong SFT baseline; and watch for length growth as a hidden objective. This page connects to the evaluation page (judge biases, human agreement), to safety (red-teaming data feeds the loop) and to agents (RL with tool use and verifiable rewards is how many agentic behaviors are now trained).
