Most eval disagreements come from unpinned details, not the model. Fix and record the prompt template, few-shot examples, answer-extraction rule, sampling parameters and number of samples; small formatting changes can swing scores noticeably (Sclar et al. 2023 documented large sensitivity to spurious prompt-format choices), and different harnesses implementing the "same" benchmark can report different numbers. A parsing failure counts as a wrong answer, so extraction bugs masquerade as capability gaps.

Treat the eval like software: version the dataset, keep a dev set for iteration and a separate locked test set, because hill-climbing on a fixed set overfits it. Compare models on identical items so that you can use paired statistics. Step 6 matters most: read a sample of raw outputs, since a metric can be high for the wrong reason (for example, a judge rewarding length).

Contamination comes in grades: exact copies, near-duplicates, paraphrases or translations, and indirect leakage (a solution post, or benchmark data in later fine-tuning sets). GPT-3's paper (Brown et al. 2020) used 13-gram overlap to flag contaminated items; n-gram matching misses paraphrases, which Yang et al. (2023) showed can inflate scores, so embedding similarity and LLM-based rephrase detection are added. Canary strings embedded in benchmark files let developers filter them from training corpora, but only if developers respect them.

Remedies: time-split evaluation on problems published after the model's training cutoff (as in continuously refreshed code benchmarks), private test sets, and reporting results with and without suspected overlap. Black-box users often cannot verify what the model saw, so treat leaderboard gains on public static sets with caution.

Zheng et al. (2023), who introduced MT-Bench and studied Chatbot Arena, found strong LLM judges agree with human preferences at roughly the level humans agree with each other, but also measured position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases. Mitigations work as follows. Swapping order and counting disagreements as ties removes position effects (and the disagreement rate itself measures judge noise). Length-controlled scoring fits a model that estimates the preference after adjusting for length difference (as in AlpacaEval's length-controlled variant, Dubois et al. 2024). Reference answers and explicit rubrics reduce subjectivity on checkable tasks.

Validate the judge like any classifier: collect a human-labeled anchor set, report agreement per category with a chance-corrected statistic, and look at where the judge errs, because overall agreement hides weak slices (for example, math correctness versus tone).

The panel formula assumes one shared success probability p. Because 1 - (1-p)^k is concave in p, plugging the average p into it overstates true pass@k (Jensen's inequality). Example: two problems with p = 1 and p = 0 have average p = 0.5, so the plug-in estimate for k=5 is 0.97, yet the correct pass@5 is 0.5.

The standard estimator (Chen et al. 2021) avoids bias: sample n ≥ k completions per problem, count c correct, and compute 1 - C(n-c, k)/C(n, k), then average over problems. Pass@k assumes an oracle that recognizes the correct sample (unit tests); a deployed system must choose one answer, via majority vote (self-consistency, Wang et al. 2022) or a verifier. And for reliability the relevant quantity is the reverse: pass^k, the probability that all k attempts succeed, which falls as k grows.

Calibration asks whether stated confidence matches frequency. Expected calibration error bins predictions by confidence and averages |accuracy - confidence| weighted by bin size. It depends on bin count and is noisy for small n, so pair it with a reliability diagram and a proper scoring rule such as the Brier score. Temperature scaling (Guo et al. 2017) fits one scalar T to rescale logits on validation data; it fixes much miscalibration without changing predictions.

For LLMs: Kadavath et al. (2022) found large pretrained models fairly well calibrated on multiple-choice questions, and the GPT-4 technical report (2023) showed post-training with RLHF degraded calibration of token probabilities. Calibration matters operationally for selective answering: you can abstain below a confidence threshold, and the useful curve is accuracy versus coverage.

Agreement is the ceiling on what you can learn. Cohen's kappa for two raters is (p_o - p_e)/(1 - p_e), observed agreement corrected for the agreement expected by chance from the marginal label frequencies; Krippendorff's alpha generalizes to many raters, missing ratings and ordinal scales. The commonly quoted bands for "moderate" or "substantial" kappa (Landis and Koch 1977) are conventions, and kappa can be low despite high raw agreement when one category is very common (the kappa paradox).

If humans agree only 70% of the time on a task, no model-based judge can be meaningfully validated beyond that, and the rubric probably needs sharpening. For rankings from pairwise comparisons, fit a Bradley-Terry or Elo-style model (as Chatbot Arena does, Chiang et al. 2024) and report intervals on the ratings.

Report uncertainty at the level of the difference. For accuracy p on n items, the standard error is √(p(1-p)/n); the panel's "±3.2" at 78% implies roughly n = 640 items. With few items or extreme accuracies, prefer a Wilson interval, which behaves better than the normal approximation near 0 or 1. Overlapping CIs do not prove no difference: when models run on the same questions, errors are correlated, and a paired analysis (the per-item difference, with a paired bootstrap or McNemar's test) is more powerful.

Items that share a passage or source are not independent, so resample clusters. Also separate sources of noise: sampling randomness (re-run with multiple seeds), prompt sensitivity, and finite test-set size. Miller (2024) laid out this statistical treatment for language-model evals.

A taxonomy is only useful if it drives the fix. Sample failures (for example 100), label each with one primary category, and count: the Pareto chart tells you where effort pays. To attribute causes you need controlled interventions. Give the model oracle retrieved passages: if accuracy jumps, retrieval was the bottleneck; if not, the problem is reading or reasoning. Feed correct tool arguments to separate tool-selection errors from tool-use errors. Evaluate at both outcome level (was the final answer right?) and trace level (were intermediate steps valid?), since agents can reach correct answers through flawed steps.

Refusal needs two-sided measurement: over-refusal on benign but edgy requests (for example the XSTest suite, Röttger et al. 2023) and under-refusal on genuinely harmful ones, reported separately because optimizing one tends to worsen the other.
ml-llm-production-04.further: Misconceptions: a high benchmark score is not a user-experience guarantee, an LLM judge is not ground truth, and a leaderboard rank difference of one point is usually noise. Gotchas: evals saturate (once models score 95%, remaining errors are often label errors), so keep refreshing difficulty; aggregate scores hide regressions on slices, so report per-slice results; and changing the sampling temperature or prompt between models invalidates a comparison. This page applies the foundations pages (confidence intervals, leakage, calibration) to LLMs. The alignment page depends on judge quality, and the system-design page needs an offline eval plus online monitoring that share definitions of success.

panels: Hoffmann et al. (2022) fit training loss as L(N, D) = E + A/N^α + B/D^β, where E is irreducible loss, with exponents near 0.3 for both. Minimizing under a compute budget C ≈ 6ND leads to N and D growing roughly in proportion, giving the ~20 tokens-per-parameter rule: their 70B-parameter Chinchilla model trained on about 1.4T tokens outperformed the 280B Gopher trained on about 300B tokens using similar compute. This revised earlier guidance (Kaplan et al. 2020) that favored growing parameters faster than data. Compute-optimal here concerns training cost only. If a model will serve large inference volume, a smaller model trained on many more tokens can be cheaper in total (Sardana and Frankle 2023), which is why many deployed models are trained far beyond 20 tokens per parameter.

The 6ND count decomposes as: forward pass 2ND (each parameter does one multiply and one add per token), backward pass 4ND (2ND to get gradients with respect to activations and another 2ND for gradients with respect to weights). The backward pass costs twice the forward pass because it computes two sets of gradients. Sanity check with a known number: GPT-3, 175B parameters on 300B tokens, gives 6 × 1.75e11 × 3e11 ≈ 3.15e23 FLOPs, matching the reported figure of about 3.14e23.

The approximation omits the attention-score computation, which adds a term growing with context length (it matters when context is comparable to model width). For mixture-of-experts models use active parameters per token, not total. With activation checkpointing, the forward pass is repeated, so hardware executes about 8ND while the useful model FLOPs stay 6ND.

The 8N-byte floor assumes weights, gradients and both Adam moments all stored in bf16 (2 bytes each). Standard mixed-precision training is larger: bf16 weights (2) and gradients (2) for compute, plus fp32 master weights (4) and fp32 Adam m and v (4 + 4) for stability, giving 16 bytes per parameter (the accounting used in the ZeRO paper, Rajbhandari et al. 2020). A 70B model then needs about 1.1 TB for persistent state alone, far beyond one GPU, which is why states are sharded: ZeRO stage 1 shards optimizer states across data-parallel ranks, stage 2 also gradients, stage 3 also parameters (the idea behind FSDP).

Activations come on top, scaling with batch × sequence × width. Activation checkpointing stores only layer boundaries and recomputes the rest, trading roughly 33% more compute for large memory savings.

The formula should use KV heads, not attention heads, for H. For a 7B-class model with full multi-head attention (32 layers, 32 heads, head dimension 128), the cache is 2 × 32 × 32 × 128 × 2 bytes = 524,288 bytes, or 0.5 MiB per cached token. Weights are about 14 GB, so cache equals weights at roughly 27,000 cached tokens (summed over all concurrent requests). For 70B with GQA (80 layers, 8 KV heads, head dim 128) the cache is 320 KiB per token while weights are 140 GB, so the crossover is near 430,000 tokens total.

So "weights dominate" holds at small total tokens in flight, and "cache dominates" at long context or high concurrency; the transition depends on architecture. Levers: GQA or latent attention, cache quantization, and sliding-window attention all shrink it.

MFU, popularized by the PaLM paper (Chowdhery et al. 2022, which reported about 46% for its 540B model on TPU v4), is useful FLOPs divided by peak. Compute it concretely: MFU = (tokens per second × 6N) / (number of GPUs × peak FLOPs per GPU), where peak is the dense figure for the datatype in use (about 990 TFLOPs for H100 bf16, not the sparse figure). Hardware FLOPs utilization (HFU) also counts recomputation, so it is higher than MFU when checkpointing is on.

Good MFU is relative to scale and hardware. Large dense-model runs commonly report somewhere around 30-50%, and above 50-60% is rare. Improving it is mostly systems work: fused kernels and FlashAttention, overlapping communication with compute, larger micro-batches to amortize overheads, balanced pipeline stages to shrink bubbles, and eliminating data-loading stalls.

Notice how the ladder compounds unit conversions. The worked example gives 1.4e8 seconds, about 1,620 days on a single 1 PFLOP/s device at 30% MFU. Spreading over n devices divides the time by n if scaling were perfect: Time ≈ 6ND / (n × peak × MFU), so 1,024 such devices would take roughly 1.4e5 seconds, about 1.6 days. Converting to cost: GPU-hours = 4.2e22 / (1e15 × 0.3 × 3600) ≈ 39,000, which at an assumed $2 per GPU-hour is about $78,000 for the compute of one such run, before experiments, failures and evaluation.

What the ladder omits: restarts and failures at cluster scale (effective goodput below MFU), data pipeline, evaluation, and the many smaller runs used for ablations and scaling-law fits, which commonly cost a large multiple of the final run.

On a log-log plot, loss versus compute looks like a straight line only after subtracting the irreducible term; otherwise the curve flattens toward E. Small-scale runs let you fit the curve and extrapolate: the GPT-4 technical report (2023) stated that final loss was predicted from runs using a tiny fraction of the compute. Extrapolation is risky: exponents shift with data quality, architecture and the range fit, and loss improvements need not map smoothly to capabilities.

Whether capabilities appear "emergently" (Wei et al. 2022) or only look abrupt because of discontinuous metrics (Schaeffer et al. 2023) is debated. Another axis is inference-time compute: sampling more, or reasoning longer, improves some tasks and gives a second scaling dimension (Snell et al. 2024). Better data, algorithms and synthetic data can move the frontier; their limits are not well established.

Napkin discipline is partly about error propagation: relative errors multiply, so several inputs each uncertain by 2x can leave the answer off by 10x or more. Vary the dominant input to get a range, not a point. Know the usual unit traps: bits versus bytes; GB (1e9) versus GiB (2^30, about 7% larger); dense versus sparse peak FLOPs; bf16 versus fp8 peaks (the latter roughly double); total versus active parameters for mixture-of-experts.

Validate against anchors you know: GPT-3 about 3.1e23 FLOPs; a bf16 70B model about 140 GB; a 7B model about 14 GB. If your result for a similar model is wildly different, find the error before presenting. In an interview, narrate: goal, assumptions, formula, numbers with units, result, then a sanity check and what would change it.
ml-llm-internals-04.further: Misconceptions: scaling laws are empirical fits, not physical laws; they describe loss on a given data distribution and recipe, not guaranteed downstream abilities. Chinchilla-optimal is not "best" for products with heavy inference. Gotchas: parameters, tokens and FLOPs are quoted inconsistently across papers (including or excluding embeddings, counting epochs or unique tokens), so check definitions before comparing. This page connects to serving (weights versus cache) and to distributed training (what MFU loses to communication and pipeline bubbles).

panels: The superposition hypothesis (Elhage et al. 2022, "Toy Models of Superposition") says a network can represent more features than it has dimensions by assigning features to nearly orthogonal directions rather than orthogonal axes. In n dimensions you can fit far more than n directions whose pairwise overlaps are small. The price is interference: reading out feature i by projecting onto its direction also picks up small contributions from other active features. This is tolerable only when features are sparse, meaning rarely active together, and a nonlinearity such as ReLU can then filter the noise. The consequence is polysemantic neurons, single units that respond to several unrelated features, because features are not aligned with the neuron basis. Whether real LLMs follow this picture closely is supported by evidence but not settled.

A sparse autoencoder (SAE) is trained on a model's activations x (dimension d_model) to reconstruct them through a much wider hidden layer: a = ReLU(W_enc x + b), x̂ = W_dec a, with loss ||x - x̂||² + λ||a||₁. The L1 term pushes most entries of a to zero, so each activation is explained by a few dictionary directions (columns of W_dec). Bricken et al. (2023) and Cunningham et al. (2023) showed interpretable features on small models, and Templeton et al. (2024) scaled the approach to a production Claude model. Caveats: reconstruction is imperfect (substituting the SAE output raises loss), features can split or merge as dictionary size changes, and interpretability of a feature is judged by humans or automated explanations. Whether SAE features are the model's "true" units is open.

Induction heads (Olsson et al. 2022) are a two-head circuit. A previous-token head in an earlier layer writes "my previous token was X" into each position's residual stream. An induction head in a later layer then forms its query from the current token A, matches it against those stored previous-token keys (K-composition) to find earlier positions that followed an A, attends to the token that came after, and copies it forward, boosting B. Note that it attends to the token after the earlier match, as in the panel's example where it attends to "chef".

The notable evidence is developmental: induction heads form at a sharp point early in training that coincides with a visible bump in the loss curve and a jump in in-context learning ability, and ablating them hurts in-context learning in small models.

A circuit (Olah et al. 2020) is a subgraph of the network, components plus the connections between them, that implements a behavior. A well-studied case is indirect-object identification in GPT-2 small (Wang et al. 2022), where about two dozen attention heads in several functional classes (finding repeated names, inhibiting the repeated name, moving the remaining name to the output) jointly explain a behavior such as completing "John and Mary went to the store; John gave a drink to ..." with "Mary". Automated discovery, such as ACDC (Conmy et al. 2023), prunes edges that do not affect a metric. Pitfalls: circuits are found on a narrow task distribution, models contain backup components that take over when one is ablated (the hydra effect, McGrath et al. 2023), and mapping a whole large model remains hard.

Denoising patching runs the corrupted input and inserts a clean activation at one site; recovery of the clean output shows that site is sufficient to carry the needed information. Noising patching does the reverse (insert corrupt activations into a clean run), testing necessity. The two can disagree when circuits have redundancy: a necessary-looking component may be replaceable, and a sufficient one may not be necessary. Effects are typically measured with a metric like logit difference between correct and incorrect answers, normalized so 0 is the corrupted and 1 the clean value.

Design choices matter (Zhang and Nanda 2023 discuss best practices): how corrupted inputs are made (swapping a name versus adding noise), which metric is used, and whether patched activations are off-distribution. Patching shows where information matters, not alone what it means.

Steering adds a vector at chosen layers during the forward pass: x' = x + λd. A direction d is commonly built from a difference of mean activations between contrasting prompts (activation addition, Turner et al. 2023; contrastive activation addition, Rimsky et al. 2023; representation engineering, Zou et al. 2023), or from an SAE feature, as in the "Golden Gate Claude" demonstration (Anthropic 2024), where amplifying one feature made the model keep bringing up the bridge. The opposite operation is also informative: Arditi et al. (2024) found that refusal behavior in several open chat models is largely mediated by one direction, and removing it disables refusals, which also means refusal can be fragile.

Practice: sweep the layer and coefficient; effect is typically non-monotonic, with too large a λ producing incoherent text.

Treat the rungs as increasing evidence about different claims. Correlation (a probe or a feature that tracks Y) shows information is present, not that the model uses it: Hewitt and Liang (2019) showed that powerful probes can decode properties from representations through their own capacity, which motivated control tasks. Ablation tests necessity but depends on what you replace the activation with: zero ablation can push the model off-distribution; mean ablation and resample ablation (substituting activations from other inputs) are less disruptive but not neutral. Even a successful intervention may not mean the model uses the direction naturally; it may only be a lever. Interpretability illusions are documented (Bolukbasi et al. 2021 found that subspaces that look meaningful on one dataset behaved differently on others), so replicate across data.

"Empirical reverse engineering" means each claim should have a prediction that could fail. Strong evidence typically combines several methods agreeing: a feature found by SAE, whose ablation changes behavior as predicted, whose steering does the opposite, and which holds on held-out data. Run sanity checks for the method itself: Adebayo et al. (2018) showed that some popular saliency maps barely change when the model's weights are randomized, so appealing pictures need a null test. Avoid anthropomorphic shorthand such as "the model wants" or "believes": a feature is a direction that correlates with and influences computations, nothing more. State what is not established: interpretability results on small models or narrow tasks need not transfer, completeness (explaining all of a behavior, rather than some) is rarely achieved, and scaling analysis to frontier models is an active, unsettled research problem.
ml-llm-internals-07.further: Misconceptions: finding a feature that fires on a concept does not show the model uses it, attention maps are not explanations, and an SAE feature with a clean label is not guaranteed to be a natural unit of the model. Gotchas: results depend on the dataset used to find features, patching requires well-matched clean and corrupt inputs, and steering strength is easy to overtune. Connections: the residual stream and attention structure here come from the transformer page; the correlation-versus-causation ladder is the same logic as the foundations page on causality, applied to a network via interventions; and safety work uses these tools for auditing behaviors (for instance, probing for deception-related features) with the caveat that auditing evidence is partial.

panels:
The map is a threat model: list what must be protected (user data, funds, reputation, third parties) and the paths by which an attacker, or a mistake, can reach them. The model is one component among several; most severe incidents in deployed LLM systems come from combining a modest model failure with excessive permissions. Simon Willison's "lethal trifecta" is a useful heuristic: an agent that has access to private data, is exposed to untrusted content, and can communicate externally can be induced to leak that data. Remove any one leg and the risk drops sharply.

Defense in depth follows the Swiss-cheese model (Reason 1990): each layer has holes, and harm happens only when the holes line up, so layers need independent failure modes.

In a transformer all text, system prompt and web page alike, is one token sequence; no hardware privilege separation exists. Wallace et al. (2024) trained models to follow higher-privilege instructions when they conflict with lower ones, and this improves robustness but remains probabilistic, so it must not be treated as a security guarantee. Direct injection ('ignore previous instructions', Perez and Ribeiro 2022) comes from the user; indirect injection (Greshake et al. 2023) hides instructions in content the model retrieves, such as a web page or email.

Architectural approaches move control decisions out of the model: for example, systems where the model that sees untrusted text has no tool access and a privileged planner works only on trusted input, or designs that track data provenance through the program (CaMeL, Debenedetti et al. 2025).

The key move is enforcing policy in deterministic code outside the model. Examples: a tool allowlist with typed argument schemas; scoping credentials per task and per user (so a hijacked agent only has that user's access); egress controls that restrict which domains the system may contact; and a confirmation step for irreversible or costly actions that shows the user the actual action rather than the model's description. A well-known exfiltration channel is rendered content: if a chat interface auto-loads a markdown image URL that contains private data in the query string, injected instructions can leak it without any tool call. Output validation applies to both directions: scan for secrets and personal data before display, and validate model-produced structured calls against schemas before execution.

A safety rubric turns values into testable statements: harm categories, severity levels, what counts as a failure, and what thresholds block launch. Red-teaming (Ganguli et al. 2022) uses people, and increasingly other models (Perez et al. 2022), to search for failures; the set of attacks found is a lower bound, not a coverage guarantee. Keep a regression suite of every past failure so fixes cannot silently regress, and separate it from held-out attack sets, otherwise you overfit defenses to known attacks.

If you observe zero failures in n independent trials, the 95% upper bound on the failure rate is about 3/n (the rule of three), so 0 of 1,000 only shows the rate is likely below 0.3%. Measure both attack success rate and false-block rate on benign traffic, and rerun after every model, prompt or tool change.

There is no single dial from permissive to restrictive; there are two error types. Over-refusal wastes legitimate users' time and erodes trust (Röttger et al. 2023 built XSTest to measure it with benign prompts that resemble harmful ones); under-refusal enables harm. Assess a request by plausible user population, severity of worst-case harm, counterfactual uplift (is the information freely available?), and context supplied by operator and user.

Good behavior is often not binary refusal: answer the safe part, offer high-level or protective information, ask a clarifying question, or point to appropriate resources. Consistency matters because users probe by rephrasing, so a policy that flips on trivial wording changes is both unsafe and annoying. Evaluate with paired sets, harmful requests and look-alike benign requests, and track both rates together as a trade-off curve rather than a single score.

Layers help only if their failures are not correlated. A safety classifier built from the same base model as the assistant may share its blind spots, and an attack that fools one may fool both. Combine different mechanisms: policy in code, classifiers, sandboxing, quotas, humans. Sandboxing means default-deny: no network egress, read-only or scoped file systems, resource and time limits, and fresh environments per session, because model-written code is untrusted code. Allowlists should validate arguments, not just tool names.

Tamper-evident audit logs (for example append-only storage with hash chaining) support forensics, and rate limits bound the damage of any one failure and also deter large-scale abuse and cost attacks. Decide failure mode explicitly: fail closed for high-risk actions (if the guard is down, do not act), fail open only where harm is minimal.

Capability-scaled safety is formalized in frontier safety frameworks, such as Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy (with AI Safety Levels), OpenAI's Preparedness Framework and Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework. The common structure: define capability thresholds in risk areas (for example biological, cyber, autonomy), run evaluations to detect them, and require stronger safeguards before deployment or further scaling once a threshold is reached or evaluations cannot rule it out.

Two difficulties. First, elicitation: a failed evaluation shows only that your prompts did not reveal the capability; better scaffolding, fine-tuning or tool access can raise measured ability, so evaluations should use strong elicitation and leave a safety margin. Second, risk depends on affordances, not just model intelligence: the same model with code execution, browsing and payment tools has a different risk profile than a text-only one.

Define severity levels in advance, with owners and response times; track time to detect and time to contain. Containment tools for LLM systems are mostly system-level: feature flags to disable a tool or capability, a kill switch for a specific agent action, rollback of a prompt or model version, tightened filters, and revoking credentials. Changing model weights is slow, so plan for mitigation at faster layers first and a proper fix later.

Root-cause analysis should be blameless and aim at contributing conditions: a missing permission boundary is more actionable than 'the model misbehaved.' Convert each incident into a regression test and, where relevant, a monitoring rule. Preserve evidence (prompts, retrieved documents, tool calls) subject to privacy and retention rules, and define who communicates with affected users and when, including any legal disclosure obligations.
ml-llm-production-05.further: Misconceptions: a safety-trained model is not a secured system, a system prompt saying 'never do X' is not an access control, and a filter with 99% recall can still fail badly under adaptive attack because attackers choose inputs after seeing outputs. Gotchas: evaluating only single-turn prompts misses multi-turn and tool-mediated attacks; success on a public jailbreak list says little about novel attacks; and over-logging creates its own privacy risk. This page builds on the alignment page (training for refusal behavior), the agents page (tool permissions and injection are most acute for agents), and the evaluation page (measuring rare failures and judge reliability). The consistent theme is to assume the model can be manipulated, then limit what manipulation can achieve.

Every replica starts from identical weights and sees a different slice of the batch, so averaging gradients reproduces large-batch SGD exactly (up to floating-point order). A ring all-reduce moves about 2(n-1)/n times the gradient size per GPU, which is nearly independent of the number of GPUs n; so communication time depends on model size and link bandwidth, not on how many replicas you add. Frameworks hide latency by grouping gradients into buckets and starting all-reduce during the backward pass while earlier layers are still computing.

The effective batch size is per-GPU batch × GPUs × gradient-accumulation steps, so scaling out changes the optimization problem and usually requires adjusting the learning rate and warmup. The main limit is memory: every GPU holds full weights, gradients and optimizer states, which is what sharding (FSDP/ZeRO) addresses.

Megatron-LM (Shoeybi et al. 2019) splits a transformer's matrices so that communication occurs only at fixed points. In an MLP the first linear layer is split by columns, so each GPU computes its own slice of the hidden activations independently (the elementwise nonlinearity needs no communication); the second layer is split by rows, producing partial sums that one all-reduce adds. So each transformer layer needs two all-reduces in the forward pass and two in the backward pass, on activation-sized tensors, directly on the critical path.

Note the distinction behind the panel's example: a column-split output is concatenated (all-gather), whereas a row-split output is summed (all-reduce). Because of the frequent, latency-sensitive communication, tensor parallelism is normally kept within one node over NVLink-class links, commonly degree 2 to 8, rather than across slower inter-node networks.

GPipe (Huang et al. 2019) splits a minibatch into m microbatches and p layer groups. In the simple schedule, each stage idles while the pipeline fills and drains, giving a bubble fraction (p-1)/(m+p-1); for the panel's p=4 and m=6 that is 3/9, about 33%, so you want m much larger than p. The 1F1B schedule (PipeDream-style; Narayanan et al. 2021 for the Megatron version) alternates one forward and one backward per stage, which does not shrink the bubble but limits how many microbatches' activations must be stored, cutting peak memory; interleaved schedules assign several smaller chunks per device to shrink the bubble further at the price of more communication.

Pipeline traffic is point-to-point activations between neighboring stages, small compared with TP all-reduces, so it tolerates slower links and is the usual choice for cross-node splits.

ZeRO (Rajbhandari et al. 2020) removes the redundancy in data parallelism in stages: stage 1 shards optimizer states, stage 2 also gradients, stage 3 also parameters. With the 16-bytes-per-parameter accounting of mixed-precision Adam, per-GPU persistent memory falls from 16Ψ toward 16Ψ/N across N data-parallel ranks. FSDP is PyTorch's implementation of the stage-3 idea: each layer's parameters are all-gathered just before use in forward, freed after, gathered again for backward, and the gradients are reduce-scattered so each rank keeps only its shard. Communication is about 1.5x that of plain data parallelism (three collectives of size Ψ versus all-reduce's two-equivalent), which is hidden by prefetching the next layer's parameters during the current layer's compute.

Tuning knobs: wrap granularity (per transformer block), prefetch, and hybrid sharding (shard within a node, replicate across nodes) to keep all-gathers on fast links.

bf16 has 8 exponent bits (the same range as fp32) but only 8 bits of significand precision, about 2-3 decimal digits; fp16 has 5 exponent bits (max 65,504) and 11 bits of significand precision. fp16 therefore needs loss scaling (multiply the loss so small gradients do not underflow, then unscale, skipping steps on overflow), while bf16 usually does not. Master weights in fp32 matter because an update such as learning rate × gradient may be 1e-5 relative to a weight of magnitude 1e-2, which a low-precision weight would round away.

FP8 training exists (Micikevicius et al. 2022 proposed the formats; DeepSeek-V3, 2024, reported using it at scale), with finer-grained scaling factors; it is newer and less standardized, so treat recipes carefully.

Activation checkpointing (Chen et al. 2016) saves only certain layer inputs and recomputes the others during backward. Storing a checkpoint every √L layers gives roughly O(√L) activation memory for L layers at the cost of one extra forward pass, i.e. up to ~33% more total compute (a forward is about a third of a training step), consistent with the panel's 10-30% when only part of the model is recomputed. Selective recomputation (Korthikanti et al. 2022) recomputes just the cheap-to-recompute but memory-heavy parts, such as attention internals, retaining most of the savings for a few percent overhead.

It interacts with randomness (dropout must use the same masks in recomputation, which frameworks handle by saving RNG state) and with MFU accounting, since recomputed FLOPs count as hardware FLOPs but not useful model FLOPs.

Useful identity: all-reduce = reduce-scatter + all-gather. In a ring algorithm with data size S on n ranks, reduce-scatter and all-gather each move (n-1)/n × S per rank, so all-reduce moves about 2S. FSDP replaces DDP's single all-reduce of gradients with two all-gathers of parameters and one reduce-scatter of gradients, hence the 1.5x traffic. Reduce-scatter leaves each rank with its own shard of the summed result, which is exactly what sharded optimizers need.

All-to-all, where every rank sends a different chunk to every other rank, is the primitive behind mixture-of-experts routing (expert parallelism) and sequence parallel schemes. Real bandwidth depends on topology: GPUs in a node connected by NVLink get several times the bandwidth of the network between nodes, so parallelism dimensions are mapped accordingly (tensor parallel within the node, data or pipeline across nodes).

Persistent state in mixed-precision Adam is about 16 bytes per parameter (bf16 weights 2 + bf16 gradients 2 + fp32 master weights 4 + fp32 m and v 8), of which the panel's "8 bytes" is just the moments. Activations for a transformer layer in 16-bit are roughly s·b·h·(34 + 5·a·s/h) bytes (Korthikanti et al. 2022), with sequence length s, batch b, hidden size h and a heads; the quadratic term disappears with fused attention kernels like FlashAttention.

One often-forgotten consumer is the logits: batch × sequence × vocabulary in fp32, for 8 × 4,096 tokens and a 128K vocabulary, is about 17 GB, so large-vocabulary models chunk the loss computation. Peaks also occur in the optimizer step or when the longest sequence arrives, so a late OOM is often just the longest batch.

First reproduce at small scale: a smaller model or fewer GPUs, so you can bisect. Use a memory timeline to see which phase peaks: forward end, backward start, or optimizer step, mapping directly to the panel's A and B branches. For OOM that appears late, suspect a leak: storing tensors that retain the autograd graph (accumulating loss without .item() or detach()), or caches growing with variable shapes.

For slowness, measure rather than guess: compute MFU, then use a profiler (PyTorch profiler or Nsight Systems) to see kernel gaps, communication wait, and data-loader stalls. One slow rank (a straggler) stalls every collective; compare per-rank step times. Hangs usually come from ranks that disagree about the next collective (different control flow or uneven data), or failing nodes; set NCCL debug logging and timeouts.
ml-llm-internals-05.further: Misconceptions: more GPUs do not guarantee proportional speedup (communication and bubbles take their share), FSDP is not model parallelism in the layer-splitting sense (it is sharded data parallelism), and bigger micro-batches are not always better because they hurt pipeline balance and memory. Large runs combine strategies: data parallelism across the cluster, tensor parallelism inside nodes, pipeline parallelism across nodes, and sharded states, a configuration often called 3D parallelism. Gotchas: numerical nondeterminism across parallel layouts, and loss spikes that need clipping, skip-batch or restart logic. This page ties to the scaling-laws page (MFU, memory accounting) and the serving page (tensor parallelism and cache reappear at inference).

panels: Real pipelines have more stages than the diagram. After normalization comes pre-tokenization, which splits text into chunks (words, punctuation, digit groups) using a regular expression, and only then does the learned subword model run within each chunk, so no token can span a pre-tokenization boundary. GPT-2 introduced byte-level BPE (Radford et al. 2019): the base alphabet is the 256 byte values, so any string, in any script or with emoji, can be encoded with no unknown token, and decoding is exactly invertible. After tokenization, each ID indexes a row of the embedding matrix (V × d_model; a 100K vocabulary at d_model=4096 is about 410M parameters), and the output layer projects back to V logits, which many models tie to the same matrix. So vocabulary size affects model size, softmax cost and sequence length together.

BPE (Sennrich et al. 2016 for translation, adapting a 1994 compression algorithm) starts with characters or bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new symbol, recording the merge order, until the vocabulary reaches a target size. Encoding then applies the learned merges in rank order to new text; it is not a longest-match search. Vocabulary size is a trade-off: larger vocabularies produce fewer tokens per text (cheaper attention and KV cache, more text per context window) but add embedding and softmax parameters and leave rare tokens seen too few times to learn well. Undertrained tokens produce odd behavior: Rumbelow and Watkins (2023) found "glitch tokens" (such as SolidGoldMagikarp) that existed in the vocabulary but were almost absent from training data, so the model responded erratically.

SentencePiece (Kudo and Richardson 2018) is a toolkit that tokenizes raw text without a language-specific pre-tokenizer, encoding the space as a visible symbol (▁) so detokenization is lossless. It supports BPE and a unigram language model (Kudo 2018). The unigram approach starts with a large candidate vocabulary and prunes pieces that least reduce corpus likelihood; at encoding time it finds the highest-probability segmentation with the Viterbi algorithm, rather than greedy longest match, and can even sample alternative segmentations during training (subword regularization) for robustness.

If untrusted user text contains the literal string of a control token, such as an end-of-turn marker, some tokenizers will parse it as the real special token, letting users forge conversation structure. Good libraries have a flag to treat special-token strings as plain text; check how yours behaves.

Most pre-tokenizers attach the leading space to the following word, so " cat" is a different token, with a different embedding, from "cat". Consequence: a prompt that ends in a trailing space forces the model into an unnatural boundary, because in training the space would have been merged into the next word; this is why a stray space at the end of a prompt can degrade completions. Numbers: some tokenizers chunk digits in groups of up to three from the left, others split every digit, so the same number has different alignment and arithmetic tasks behave differently (Singh and Strouse 2024 studied this effect). Unicode: composed and decomposed forms of the same visible character differ at the code-point level, and homoglyphs (look-alike letters) evade filters; normalize inputs consistently.

Fertility is the average number of tokens per word, and it varies by language because vocabularies are learned from training text dominated by a few languages. Studies (Petrov et al. 2023; Ahia et al. 2023) documented that some languages need several times as many tokens for equivalent content, so users pay more, hit context limits sooner, and get higher latency. Cost scales with tokens in different ways: billing and KV cache grow linearly with token count, while the attention score computation grows quadratically in sequence length, so doubling tokens roughly quadruples that part. Tokenizer-free alternatives that operate on bytes with learned patching or hierarchy exist (for example the Byte Latent Transformer, Pagnoni et al. 2024), but subword tokenization remains the production default; whether it will be replaced is unsettled.

Embedding row k means nothing in a different vocabulary, so the tokenizer is effectively part of the model's weights. Chat templates specify exactly how role names, message boundaries and end-of-turn tokens are inserted; fine-tuning and inference must use the same template as training of the instruction-tuned model. Subtle template bugs: duplicated beginning-of-sequence tokens (the template adds one and the tokenizer adds another), a missing end-of-sequence token in fine-tuning data (the model learns never to stop), tokenizing the template text as plain text instead of special tokens, and masking the loss on the wrong span.

For batched generation with decoder-only models, pad on the left so the last real token is adjacent to the generation position. If you add special tokens to a vocabulary, resize the embedding matrix and initialize the new rows sensibly; they are untrained.

Round-trip: decode(encode(text)) should reproduce text, but normalization can legitimately change it, so know which differences are expected. Compare your local token count with the provider's reported usage field; discrepancies usually mean you missed template tokens or tool schemas, which count against the context. The budget arithmetic in the panel is right: 1,842 + 1,024 = 2,866, plus a 200 buffer is 3,066, which is under 4,096. Streaming adds a subtle issue: a single character in UTF-8 can span several bytes, and byte-level tokens can split it, so decoding token by token may produce replacement characters; buffer incomplete sequences. Pin tokenizer versions (vocabulary or regex changes silently alter counts and model behavior), include tokenizer files in your model artifacts, and when behavior seems irrational on a specific input, first look at how that input was tokenized.
ml-llm-internals-02.further: Misconceptions: tokens are not words, a token is not a fixed number of characters, and the tokenizer is not a neutral preprocessing detail; it shapes cost, fairness across languages, arithmetic ability and security (special-token injection). Gotchas: whitespace and Unicode normalization differences between your data pipeline and the tokenizer, different tokenizers for the same model family across versions, and counting tokens without the chat template. This page connects to the transformer page (embedding matrix and sequence length drive memory), the serving page (token count sets KV cache and latency), the evaluation page (prompt formatting sensitivity), and the safety page (control tokens inside untrusted text).

This loop is the pattern formalized as ReAct (Yao et al. 2022), where the model interleaves reasoning text with tool calls and observations. In practice it is a program, not a prompt: a controller sends the conversation to the model, executes any requested tool, appends the result, and repeats until the model answers or a stop condition fires. Always set hard limits (maximum steps, token budget, wall-clock timeout), because loops can cycle.

Errors compound. If each step succeeds independently with probability q, an n-step task succeeds with q^n: at q = 0.95 and 20 steps, only about 36%. So reliability comes from shorter plans, validation after steps, and recovery paths. Make state explicit (an append-only event log) and record model outputs and tool results, so a failed run can be replayed deterministically without calling the model again.

Treat failures as information for the model. Return structured, actionable errors (which argument was invalid and why) as the tool result, and models can often self-correct on the next turn. Separate retryable errors (timeouts, rate limits, 5xx responses) from non-retryable ones (validation failures, permission denied); retrying the latter wastes budget and may loop. Stale state is a concurrency problem: between planning and acting, another process may have changed the data, so use version checks (compare-and-set, ETags) on writes and re-read before consequential actions.

Propagate a deadline through nested calls so a slow dependency cannot consume the whole budget. Treat tool outputs as untrusted input: a web page or email returned by a tool may contain instructions aimed at the model (indirect prompt injection), so it must not be allowed to expand the agent's permissions.

Idempotency means a repeated request has the same effect as one. For side-effecting tools, have the caller generate a unique idempotency key per logical action and have the server store results by key, so a retry after a timeout (when you do not know whether the first attempt succeeded) cannot double-charge or double-cancel. Retries should use exponential backoff with jitter (randomized delay) to avoid synchronized retry storms, with a cap on attempts; circuit breakers stop calling a failing dependency for a cooldown.

Tool descriptions are part of the prompt: the model chooses tools by reading them. Prefer a small set of clearly named, non-overlapping tools; document side effects and when not to use each; return concise, relevant output. Strict-mode schemas and constrained decoding guarantee well-formed arguments, not correct ones.

Context is a finite budget: more tokens cost more, add latency, and can reduce answer quality by diluting attention with irrelevant material (Shi et al. 2023 showed that irrelevant context can degrade accuracy). Practical tactics: compaction (summarize older turns, keeping decisions, open questions and key identifiers); an external scratchpad or notes the agent reads back when needed; truncating or paginating large tool outputs; and delegating to sub-agents that work in their own context and return only a summary.

The panel's hierarchy is a priority order, not necessarily a position: for caching you want stable material (system prompt, tool definitions) at the start, and for attention you want the current goal and the latest evidence near the end.

Liu et al. (2023, published 2024) varied where the relevant document sat among distractors in multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval: accuracy was highest when it was at the beginning or end and dropped when it was in the middle, a U-shaped curve. Simple needle-in-a-haystack tests flatter models because finding a unique sentence is easier than combining several facts; benchmarks like RULER (Hsieh et al. 2024) found effective lengths well below advertised ones for many models.

Mitigations beyond ordering: retrieve fewer, better passages and rerank; repeat key instructions at the end; ask the model to quote the relevant evidence before answering; and test your own task at your own context lengths rather than relying on published numbers.

Provider prompt caching reuses the precomputed key-value state for a prefix of the input that exactly matches an earlier request. It saves prefill compute, so it improves time to first token and input cost, but not decode speed. Because matching is token-by-token from the start, any change early in the prompt, such as a timestamp or user name placed above the instructions, invalidates everything after it. So order content from most stable to least: system prompt, tool definitions, reference documents, then conversation, then the new message. Pricing and rules differ by provider: typically cached reads are discounted steeply, writes may carry a premium, entries expire after minutes of inactivity, and a minimum prefix length applies. The same idea exists in self-hosted serving as automatic prefix caching (for example RadixAttention in SGLang, Zheng et al. 2023).

RAG (Lewis et al. 2020) quality is bounded by retrieval: if the right passage is not in the top-k, no generator can recover it. So evaluate retrieval separately with labeled queries (recall@k, MRR, nDCG) and generation separately (is the answer faithful to the retrieved context? is it relevant?). Chunking is a recall-precision trade-off: small chunks match precisely but lose context; large chunks carry context but dilute the embedding; common choices are a few hundred tokens with structure-aware boundaries (headings, sections) and some overlap. Hybrid retrieval combines lexical BM25 (good at exact names, codes, rare terms) with dense embeddings (good at paraphrase), commonly fused with reciprocal rank fusion; a cross-encoder reranker then scores query-passage pairs jointly on the shortlist, improving precision at extra latency.

RAG fails by construction in several cases. Aggregation questions (how many tickets mention X? total spend by region?) need computation over all records, which top-k similarity cannot provide; use a structured query tool (SQL) instead. Multi-hop questions require evidence from several documents connected by an intermediate fact; single-shot retrieval misses the second hop, so an agent that searches iteratively does better. If the corpus is small (say, tens of thousands of tokens) and stable, putting it all in the context, especially with prompt caching, can be simpler, cheaper to build and more accurate than a retrieval pipeline.

Retrieval can also reduce quality: irrelevant or conflicting passages can pull the model away from a correct answer it already knew. Measure RAG against a no-retrieval baseline and against long-context. If retrieval rarely changes the answer, you are paying latency for nothing.
ml-llm-production-03.further: Misconceptions: an agent is not just a bigger prompt (it is a controller with limits, state and validation); long context does not remove the need for retrieval or summarization; and prompt caching does not change model outputs, only cost and speed. Gotchas: evaluating agents by final answer only hides unsafe or wasteful intermediate steps, so log traces; tool results are an injection channel; and every added tool adds selection errors, so prune tools. This page leans on the transformer and serving pages (KV cache and prefill explain caching), the evaluation page (error taxonomy: retrieval, tool use), and the safety page (least privilege, confirmation for consequential actions). It feeds directly into the support-agent design page.

The tree orders interventions by cost and iteration speed, and separates two different needs: knowledge (what the model should know right now) versus behavior (how it should act). Knowledge that is private, frequently changing, or needs attribution belongs in retrieval; Ovadia et al. (2023) compared fine-tuning and retrieval for injecting knowledge and found retrieval generally better, especially for new facts. Behavior (format, tone, decision style) is shaped by prompts first and by fine-tuning when prompts become too long, inconsistent or costly.

Build an evaluation set before choosing, so each intervention's gain is measured against a prompt baseline. And remember that the options combine: a common production system is a prompted model with retrieval and a fine-tuned or distilled component for a high-volume, narrow step.

In-context examples work well but are sensitive to details: the choice, order and label balance of few-shot examples can swing accuracy (Zhao et al. 2021 documented majority-label and recency biases; Lu et al. 2022 showed order sensitivity), so select examples to match the task distribution and test permutations. Structured output via constrained decoding guarantees syntax (valid JSON matching a schema) but not truth: the fields can be well-formed and wrong.

Treat prompts as code: version them, keep a regression suite, and rerun it when the underlying model version changes, since behavior shifts between versions. The brittleness at scale named in the panel is real but measurable: sample failures, add targeted instructions or examples, and check that the fix does not break other cases.

Grounding raises the odds of correct answers but does not guarantee them. Models can ignore the supplied context, blend it with remembered knowledge, or misread a passage; faithfulness (answer supported by retrieved text) must be evaluated explicitly, for example by checking each claim against the cited passage. Advantages beyond freshness: access control (retrieve only documents the user may see, with filtering applied before ranking), auditability (citations), and easy knowledge updates (re-index a document, no retraining). The costs are an extra system to run: ingestion, chunking, an index, embedding model versioning, reranker latency, and monitoring for stale or missing sources. 'Evaluation that matches real use' means a test set of actual user questions with known supporting documents, not synthetic questions generated from the chunks themselves, which are easier than real ones.

It is effective for format adherence, tone, classification heuristics, and domain conventions, and often needs only hundreds to a few thousand high-quality examples for these; data quality matters far more than quantity. It is a weak way to add facts: the model may learn the surface style of an answer without reliably storing the fact, and training on facts the base model does not know has been reported to increase hallucination (Gekhman et al. 2024). Operational points: the fine-tuned model is tied to its base version, so a base upgrade means retraining and re-evaluating; fine-tuning can erode general abilities (catastrophic forgetting), so test on general benchmarks and your own prompts; the evaluation set must be disjoint and deduplicated from the training set; and hosted fine-tuned models may carry different pricing or capacity limits.

LoRA (Hu et al. 2021) freezes the pretrained weight W (d × k) and learns a low-rank update ΔW = (α/r)·B·A, where B is d × r, A is r × k, and the rank r is small (often 8 to 64). Parameter count drops from d·k to r·(d + k): for d = k = 4096 and r = 16, that is about 131K instead of 16.8M per matrix, under 1%. Because the update is additive, the adapter can be merged into W after training (no extra inference latency) or kept separate so one base model serves many adapters, which suits multi-tenant serving (S-LoRA, Sheng et al. 2023). Trade-off: Biderman et al. (2024) found that LoRA tends to learn less than full fine-tuning on harder, domain-shifting tasks but also forgets less of the base abilities.

QLoRA (Dettmers et al. 2023) stores the frozen base model in 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), a data type designed for normally distributed weights, applies double quantization (quantizing the quantization constants) to save more memory, and uses paged optimizers to survive memory spikes. During training, base weights are dequantized on the fly for each matmul and gradients flow into LoRA adapters kept in 16-bit. The paper fine-tuned a 65B-parameter model on a single 48 GB GPU, since 4-bit weights need about half a byte per parameter.

Trade-offs: each step is slower than 16-bit LoRA because of dequantization; there is a small quantization error baked into the base, which the paper reported was largely recovered by the adapters; and merging an adapter into a quantized base needs care, because requantizing after merging adds rounding error.

The table compares up-front costs, but decisions turn on the total over volume: total cost = fixed cost + N × cost per request. Fine-tuning has a fixed training and data-curation cost and can reduce the per-request cost (shorter prompts, smaller model); break-even volume = fixed cost / savings per request. For example, replacing a 3,000-token prompt with a 300-token one saves 2,700 input tokens per call, which matters at millions of calls, but less if prompt caching already discounts the long prefix. RAG has smaller fixed costs but recurring ones: index storage, embedding, retrieval latency, and the extra tokens of retrieved context on every call.

Include hidden costs: data labeling and review (often the dominant cost for fine-tuning), evaluation, re-training when the base model changes, and engineering maintenance.

Data issues: deduplicate, check labels on a sample, remove contradictory examples, and log provenance and versions. Retrieval: inspect actual retrieved chunks for failing queries before changing the model (most 'hallucinations' in RAG systems start as retrieval misses), and filter by metadata such as date and product. Fine-tuning overfit shows as validation loss rising while training loss falls, or outputs copying training phrases; mitigate with early stopping, lower rank or learning rate, and more varied data.

A frequent silent failure is mismatch: an index built with one embedding model queried with another; a fine-tuning chat template that differs from inference; or a stale index serving outdated policy. Version the whole bundle (prompt, index snapshot, adapter, base model) and tie each eval result to it.
ml-llm-production-01.further: Misconceptions: fine-tuning is not a way to teach a model your documents, RAG does not eliminate hallucination, and prompting is not 'just' a prototype technique, since strong prompting plus evaluation covers many production tasks. Gotchas: embedding model upgrades require re-indexing everything; evaluation sets leak into training data over time; and LoRA adapters are tied to the exact base weights. Connections: the alignment page explains what fine-tuning methods optimize; the evaluation page covers building the test set this decision depends on; the agents page covers RAG as a component and the cost of context; and the support-agent page applies the choice in a full system.

The dashboard's 1.8M messages per day averages about 21 per second; peaks may be 5 to 10 times the average, so plan for 100-200 requests per second. By Little's law (concurrent requests = arrival rate × time in system), 100 requests per second at 5 seconds each means about 500 generations in flight. Availability of 99.9% leaves about 43 minutes of downtime per 30-day month, which is why single-provider and single-region designs need fallbacks.

Split the latency budget across stages (gateway, routing, retrieval, time to first token, generation) and use streaming so users see output early; P95 targets must hold for the whole path including retrieval and tools. Define success metrics precisely: 'containment' (no human needed) can be gamed by making escalation hard, so pair it with resolution quality and recontact rate.

The pipeline separates concerns so each can scale and fail independently. Keep the request path stateless and store conversation state in a fast store with expiry; deduplicate inbound messages by message ID, since channels like WhatsApp retry webhooks. Put cheap work first: the router uses a small model or classifier to detect intent, language and risk, so most traffic never touches the large model. Observability and evaluation run off the request path via queues, so a slow logging system cannot add latency or take down chat.

Models, retrieval index, and tool backends will each degrade differently; add timeouts, circuit breakers and a fallback chain. Use backpressure and load shedding (reject or degrade low-priority traffic) rather than letting queues grow without bound, since long queues violate the latency SLO anyway.

A useful framing is risk = action sensitivity × probability of error. Use signals to estimate confidence: classifier probability, retrieval scores (is there a strong supporting document?), agreement across samples or models, and the model's own uncertainty. Calibrate thresholds on labeled data to meet a precision target for auto-resolution rather than guessing, and re-check after changes.

For authenticated flows, separate reading from writing and require step-up verification before sensitive actions. Policies with money or legal effect (refund limits, eligibility rules) should live in deterministic code or a rules engine that the model calls, not in the prompt. Escalate on explicit request, repeated failure, detected frustration, safety or legal categories, and high-value accounts. A good handoff packet contains the summary, the actions already tried, and retrieved articles, so the customer does not repeat themselves.

Knowledge systems fail on permissions and freshness more often than on embeddings. Access control must be enforced at retrieval time: store ACL metadata with each chunk and filter before ranking, never after generation. Version each source (product, region, effective date) so the system can prefer the correct policy version, and propagate deletions to the index to honor erasure requests. Measure retrieval with a labeled set of real queries (recall@k) in each major language; multilingual retrieval can use multilingual embeddings or translate queries, and the choice should be tested per language.

Query rewriting turns chatty multi-turn messages into standalone search queries. Citations should link to the exact section, and ideally verify that quoted text appears in the source, since fabricated citations are worse than none.

In the sample schema, the idempotent flag in practice means the server accepts an idempotency key, or the operation is naturally safe to repeat, such as cancelling an already-cancelled order, and the preconditions are checked (order status, cancellation window) in code. Most important is how identity flows: the order_id comes from the model, but the user identity must come from the authenticated session, never from model output, so the tool checks that this order belongs to this user. Otherwise a confused-deputy attack can cancel someone else's order through a manipulated prompt.

High-impact calls should require an explicit user confirmation that displays the real parameters. Fallbacks should degrade gracefully (cache, smaller model, template reply, human) and be tested regularly, because a fallback path that is never exercised tends to be broken when needed.

Privacy engineering faces a tension: the agent needs personal data to help, yet logs and prompts should not accumulate it. A common design is pseudonymization: replace identifiers with tokens before text reaches the model and logs, and detokenize only at the tool boundary where the real value is needed, under authorization. Redaction (names, emails, card numbers) must be tested on multilingual and messy text; it is a probabilistic filter, so do not rely on it as the only control. Treat user-supplied and customer-record text as untrusted: order notes, emails and attachments can contain injected instructions. Plan for data-subject requests: you need to find and delete a user's data across stores, caches and indexes, which is far easier if you designed for it from the start.

Model routing, prompt caching for the static prefix, shorter retrieved context, and output limits are the main levers. Caution on response caching: caching answers for generic FAQs is safe if keyed by language and policy version, but caching anything personalized or account-specific risks leaking one user's data or serving stale results; never share caches across users for such content. Semantic caching (matching similar questions by embedding) can return a subtly wrong answer when two questions differ in a critical detail, so use high similarity thresholds and only for low-risk intents.

Provider rate limits (requests and tokens per minute) are hard capacity constraints: secure quota in advance, spread across regions or providers, and implement priority tiers so paying or urgent traffic is served first during overload.

Containment 68% plus escalation 7.8% accounts for only about 76% of conversations; the remaining roughly 24% must be something (abandoned, unresolved, still open), and that bucket is exactly where hidden failures live. Outcome categories should be mutually exclusive and exhaustive. 'Resolved' should be validated by a signal such as no recontact within several days, not merely the user leaving. CSAT from voluntary surveys suffers response bias (extremes respond), so combine with sampled human grading; a 4.6/5 quality score needs a sample size and interval, as the evaluation page describes.

SLOs need error budgets: 99.9% availability allows 0.1% failures, and alerting on burn rate (how fast the budget is being consumed) catches problems earlier than static thresholds. Cost per resolved case should include escalated conversations and failed attempts in the numerator.

Offline evaluation checks quality, safety and tool behavior on curated and adversarial sets, but cannot predict real user behavior. Shadow mode runs the new system on mirrored traffic without showing results to users and compares outputs with the current system; it reveals latency, cost and tool errors, though not user reactions. For A/B tests, size the experiment: to detect a 2-point change in containment from a baseline of 68% with 80% power at the 5% significance level needs roughly 16·p(1-p)/δ² = 16 × 0.2176 / 0.0004, about 8,700 conversations per arm, more if you also segment. Randomize by user (not message) to avoid contamination, run through full weekly cycles, and predefine guardrail metrics (escalation, safety incidents, latency, cost).
ml-llm-production-06.further: Interview approach: clarify requirements and scale first, sketch the architecture, then go deep on two or three risk areas (retrieval and permissions, tool safety, evaluation and rollout) instead of listing every component. State assumptions and do the napkin math aloud. Common misconceptions: more automation is not always better (the right escalation rate is a product decision), a high-quality model does not replace access control, and offline evals alone do not justify full launch. Gotchas: handoff quality, multilingual regressions, stale knowledge, and provider outages.
